blocks.x: SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with
Sir Charles Thompson

Washington, D. C.
May 1975

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

Now, this is Sir Charles Thompson. This is Helen Dance interviewing Sir Charles on May 5th, 1975, and Sir Charles, we would like you to start at the very beginning with your birth date and your place of birth, and anything that you would like to tell us about your family, your mother and father. So will you start right in?
Yes. May I call you Helen?
Please.
Since we met some time ago in a very pleasant social invitation to your home, I feel that I can call you Helen without insulting your husband Stanley.
Very nice.
Thank you.
I wouldn't want it (inaudible) any other way.

So I would like to start out by saying that to my knowledge, which is illegal from my birth certificate, which I'm holding in my hand now, and it's listed as coming from the County of Clark, I believe it says here, from the State of Ohio, bureau of vital statistics, certificate of birth, which has to do with who I am. Sir Charles, who is Sir Charles Thompson? And the file number of this seems to be 21322 with a possible writing of 8 in there someplace. These papers are not always exactly clear. Some of the writing. Registration district number 175, primary registra-
tion district 8073, registration number 345. That should be enough information from that to identify this paper from the vital statistics bureau.

And my birth place was Springfield, Ohio, and my place of residence, the residence of my parents was 361 Henzo Avenue, and my full name is Charles Philip Walker Thompson, which I believe most of those names were named after people in my family who were either ministers or physicians perhaps. At least I know that one of them was a minister in the family beside my father, I believe it was on the Walker side, which is my mother. And my birth date was March the 21st, 1918. My father was Jesse L. Thompson, and my mother was Laura Walker Thompson.

And on the birth certificate which is very significant at this time of this interview, May the 5th,1975, my father is listed, his race as colored, c-o-l-o-r-e-d, something I would like to discuss in this interview. And his age was 41, my mother was also listed as colored, aged 38. My father's birth place and my mother's birth place was Mount Sterling, Kentucky. My father's occupation in industry was listed as minister, my mother's occupation in industry was interestingly enough listed as domestic. I guess that means that she took care of us because I don't remember whether she had a job or not, because She died when I was five years old, my mother, my real mother died when I was five years old. My father married again

shortly after, about a year later. He was fortunate enough to find another very kind woman who became my mother, stepmother. And I actually didn't know the difference. And from this certificate also the facts show that there were six members of the family with me, and at my birth one of my sisters had died before I was born. So this made five of us in my family which included three other sisters and a brother. Very, very vague information I have on my family. My family was quite separated, you might say, to a certain degree, not only in mind, in spirit, but in association.

Because my father was a very strict minister who devoted perhaps all of his time to the ministry. And one of the most vivid statements that he made when he passed away, he died, last year, at the age of 97, was that he always regretted that he spent all of his life trying to teach other people and help them to purify their spiritual thoughts and prepare themselves for the hereafter, whatever that the ministry has to do with. And he always regretted that he wasn't able to keep his family more together as a family.

Because most of us finally drifted away because of the very, very rigid you might say curriculum of the church and you know, this strict order of regimentation. And I happened to be the baby of the family, the last to leave.
Were you and your brothers and sisters close at all?

Well, no, not really because at the time of my birth I don't even remember knowing any of my sisters except the two who were perhaps closest to me, and that was my youngest sister, Pauline, who was just older than I am. And I knew something about the one next to her, who was already away from home and studying to become a teacher. And the first thing I remember about that sister is she was a teacher, which was years later.

I think that there was quite some confusion in the death of my mother. As I said, the combination of being brought up in a very, very Christian background of a minister's home, and the death of my mother during the period of time when I just barely can remember at the age of five, I remember some incidents which are very important. But however I can't remember any details at that age.
No. How old was your brother? I mean how much older than you was your brother?

That is one of mysteries of my life, that I don't even know the age of my brother. And we didn't discuss him too much at all because he went away from home when I was young, and I -- his whole life was very vague, and I never knew really what became of my brother officially. I do know that he was in some problems, when I was 12 years old I remember living in Colorado Springs, Colorado, and he was in some trouble that had something to do with the law.

And I remember either some detectives or people from some institution came to take my brother away, and I remember seeing him vaguely during that period, and I remember seeing he and my father in a very violent argument. I didn't know what it was about, had no idea, and that's about the only thing I knew about my brother.

Later on when I went into some process of trying to look into it, my sisters always tried to discourage me from even finding out about my brother, which leads me to believe that something violent happened to him, or something very bad happened to my brother in his life time. I have every reason to believe that he may have been in the psychopathic ward someplace in Flint, Michigan. And these are some of the things that are very vague about my life, and has I think a lot to do with my own personality. You know. And as I said I think it has something to do with actually the personality of my father.
Perhaps with your brother was some sort of rebellion then against a very strict home upbringing?

That could have been the beginning of it, but I believe that he had some trouble with some other people. I don't know what the trouble was. As I said I -- in fact this was very interesting, because this all intrigued me all of my life. And as I grew older I even went to the trouble of trying to look up my entire family background by method of
working in the bureau of census in Washington, D. C. I was hired as a clerk typist, I was rated as a G 2. And I was considered to be very proficient as a male typist.
Was this in the army?

No, this was not in the army, this was during a period of time when I was living in Washington, D. C. And things were very tough there for jazz musicians, for any black musicians I might say, I'd go so far as to say that. It was a situation of a shortage of employment.
What year would that be around?

This was around 1949 and '50. During that period. And I had previously to that worked as a clerk typist in the navy department in Cleveland, Ohio. Things were rather rough for me as a musician, and particularly as a jazz musician. There were many times in my career, there have been many times in my career and in fact as of now I'm still having problems with economics and playing music to earn a living, you know, these sort of things.
Playing the kind of music you like to play.
Right, or any kind of music just to make a living.
Yeah.
I mean, I feel that this is a very important point in discussing my life, because I'm positive that

economics is 85 percent of the control over what happens to a person. People who are fortunate enough to have the good economical background, good home, I believe have a much better chance of having total success of doing what they want to do and making a living at it.
Right.
Of course we could discuss athletes and go into another phase of it.
Right. We ought to save this. It's a very interesting discussion, we ought to save it to -- we'll try to reach that point and bring it up. Don't you think let's go back to our --
That's a good --
-- starting point, so that we can always keep going along in a chronological pattern, then we won't miss anything.
That's a good idea.
And we'll have a logical development.
That's a good idea. Let's see what we've got up to here.
[PAUSE]
Mr. Charles, what we'd like to know is was there anybody else in your family that was musical? Where did your talent come from?
My talent I would say came directly from my mother and father. Everybody in my family was

musically inclined. Every, every child in the family was musically inclined. As I said I know very little about my brother, but all three of my sisters who are living now sing, well. And my sister Louise, who is the middle sister, was very proficient at playing the piano until she had an operation on her fingers.

So I would have to say that most of my musical start came from my mother and father. My mother, I understand, used to hold me in her lap while she played the piano. My father played enough piano to realize or have someone realize that he knew where the notes were. He didn't concentrate on playing the piano because my mother was very good playing the piano. Both of my mothers, my real mother and my step mother. I knew nothing about my real mother except having seen her in the hospital on her dying day and seeing her in the casket. However, my second mother, who was my stepmother, the woman that my father married about a year later after my mother's death, she also was a very good pianist. She was not a concert performer, the fact of the matter is I used to kid my mother, my stepmother quite a bit about the way her hands never coordinated properly. One of her hands would go down ahead of the other.
But she could play the church music, she read church music. And anyone who knows anything about church music knows that church music is one of the most difficult
types of music for a pianist to read and to play. It's comparative to the music of Bach for a discipline.
Why is that?
Because of the discipline, yes.
It's --
The way it moves, progresses with both hands or?
It's a combination of musical progression, and simplicity in a complex way. That's a very difficult statement.
Yes, it is.

But the fact of the matter is music and art are anything, particularly like today in the electronic world, there is a very difficult -- well, I can't find the word I want to use at this moment, but in other words what I'm trying to say is it's very difficult to explain anything that has anything to do with art because if you can do something it's comparatively simple to you, if you understand it. However, if you do not understand it it becomes difficult.
And you can't translate it into words.
Now, I would say I'm having difficulty now to explain why this music is difficult because I don't have the knowledge as a teacher. You see.
Yeah.
And that's what makes it difficult for
Right.

That's rather confusing. But what I'm trying to say is Bach music in fact, it seems to be classic music for a pianist to practice on, is because of the discipline of fingering. Actually these notes are to be fingered by each finger separately. Each finger has a note that it plays. And church music is somewhat similar to that. There is a lot of music that is written for the churches that has a Bach sound of this discipline. The chords are very simple, the movements are very simple, but it harmonically is right and it has to be played exactly the way it was written to give the effect of it. Because this is the effect of christian music. And it must be portrayed the same way each time they have this feeling.
Did you play church music?

I tried. I started out, but the combination of my lack of interest in christianity, and the curriculum, and as I said the rigid discipline, it rather discouraged me in church music. And I was never very good at it. As I said I've played the violin sometimes when I was kid but we're still getting a little ahead.
Yes, let's go back to your early beginning.
We have to start --
You sat on your mother's lap.

Yes, we have to start, as I said, with my birth, as a child. For me to give you exactly what I remember, I would say go back to my year when I was five years old. I remember going to the hospital to see my mother the day that she died. I don't remember the date, but I went along with my father to the hospital. I remember seeing my mother lie there in the bed and smiling. She had a beautiful personality, and that's the last thing I remember about my mother, and that she was smiling even though she was very ill. And I will have to say that at this time today I don't have all of the information, the facts, but tonight I will speak to my sisters by long distance and I will have certain things and facts to substantiate what I'm telling you now, and about what was wrong with her and all these things.

But as of that time, the only thing I remember is that she had a pleasant personality and she asked me to go get her a glass of water. And now as I see it I'm sure that my mother must have had a prewarning that she was taking her last breaths and she didn't want me in the room at that time. Because as I remember when I came back she had died. And that's the way I remember my real mother. That's the only thing I remember about my real mother.
I don't remember what she looked like, precisely, and the fact of the matter is my second mother was so kind, so
gentle, and so sweet, such a mother to me that I always remembered my first mother to look like my second mother. This was a --
That's nice.
Yes. A subconscious thought. Because my second mother was so beautiful. And when I say beautiful I'm saying beautiful as a soul, as a person.
She was a mother.

She was a beautiful mother. She took on the responsibility of all these kids that belonged to my father, and in fact I'm sure that had something to do with her marrying her. Somebody to help take care of these brats. Me being number one, perhaps, because I was the baby.
Had she any children of her own at the time?
I don't believe my mother ever had any children.
Oh.
And it's very possible that she may not have -- it's very possible that she might not have been able to have children.
Yes.
I would say that could be the case, or perhaps maybe she was too old.
Yes.

Some of these things I'll have to get from my sisters, they know a little more about this than I do because they're all older than I am and a lot of facts were kept from me. But as I said it's very important in my life that many of the facts of my family, for some reason or another, have been kept from me and I have never been able to find out these certain facts which go into who my father was, who my mother was. I don't know who my father's father was. I know that he was born I believe out of wedlock by virtue of a mixed love affair of caucasian and black and Indian prospects, you see.
Yeah.
This is something he didn't like to discuss.
No.
And he had gone through a very hard period as a boy, being raised as an orphan, and he --
Tell me where, where was he raised.

He was born in Mount Sterling, Kentucky, and from all that he has told me his boyhood life was in and around Mount Sterling, Kentucky, around in that area. His father, I believe, was a gentleman who owned a tobacco farm, and my mother or his mother, there's some vagueness about this, as I said. These are the things that I don't know which I feel may be important perhaps. There may be
some way of finding out who I am through finding out who he is.
That's right.
But there is some vagueness about my beginning and his beginning, and --
But you do know he was brought up as an orphan?
Oh, yes, this is almost a fact. I don't know who the people were --
It's very hard.

Yes. My father had a very tough life when he was a boy, he's told me some about it, which included the fact that he picked tobacco as a boy, and he had very strong hands from this. My father was about my size, a little heavier than me, about 10 or 15 pounds heavier at my heaviest. Very small but strong character.
How heavy would that be?
I think my father's top weight was about 145.
Right.

Perhaps 150. I remember his top weight being about 145. A very good man, very, very devoted to his obligation to the family. And very devoted to the ministry. He went into the ministry after having had this tough life and the fact of the matter is he used to joke about it. He used to be in a lot of fights when he was a boy. Most of them I guess were started by the other party to protect himself, and

I think his mother -- the woman who raised him taught him to protect himself. In those days he -- I guess this was common teaching for a boy to protect himself in this world that he was living in that was so rough.
Yeah. How old would he have been when he picked tobacco?

Oh, I don't know, I would imagine, say perhaps 15, 16, somewhere along in there. Because he started preaching, I understand, when he was very young, probably 20 or in the early 20's. He taught school. My father put himself through school and he taught school for a short time. He was a teacher, yes. And then he decided he could do the world some good by trying to help others and he got the spiritual vision that he was a disciple of the Lord. And he decided to become a minister.
Did he get a church of his own?
Oh, yes. My father was associated with the Methodist Church.
The AME?
No, the Methodists.
Oh, I see.
Which is considered to be -- well, during the time of my childhood I accepted this to be one of the more cultural cults.
Right.

Of Christianity. Very strict in order and discipline and morals and so forth, in fact there was always a lot of controversy about the Baptists and the Catholics or the protestants and the Catholics about -- in those days there was that discussion because I remember as a child hearing that the Catholics allowed card playing and certain things of recreation that the Protestants, particularly Methodists, did not allow. You know.
Yes.

But getting back to this early childhood, I remember that and then about my mother being in the hospital, then later on during that same period I remember trying to climb up on the casket in the home where the body was for viewing, and you know. And I remember just as well as if it was yesterday, I climbed up on the casket and fell in the process, which naturally caused a lot of commotion in the house during the days of this -- before the ceremonial procedures for the funeral. And during that same period crawling on the floor I put my face on a red hot stove. Now, this I don't understand how this happened and how there's not a scar, there's not a mark on my face. I don't know how this happened. But I crawled into this red hot stove. I remember seeing these stoves in the old days where you used coal around --
Pot belly stove?

Pot belly stove, that's what they used in those days in my house, in one of these houses that my father lived in. You mentioned did he have his own church. In the Methodist religion you were sent each year you were sent to a different charge, or maybe sometimes to be kept by a certain charge. Charge means the church. And this was done by process of meetings. They had quarterly meetings, they had yearly meetings, and they would have these conferences, yearly conference, and they had the bishop who was the big man, and they had superintendents, and all these people with -- who would visit the church, it was done in a highly, orderly fashion --
Organized.

Yes. And this would decide where the minister was going to be, how well he was doing at a certain church, how well he got along with the people, how much money there was being paid off the mortgages, and so forth. And this had to do with how we lived, and also had some bearing on my life because my father being a very stern man, very, very hard to bend, he refused to get away from the rules. And he was known to be very, very technical person who insisted that the congregation do what they were supposed to do, and respect the rules of the Methodist church.
And then in the process he was known to be a very, very efficient person in paying off mortgages of churches.
And so for this reason my father --
A very valuable asset to the church, I'm sure.

Yes. But by the same process, some of the -- the people didn't like him too well, and he was moved perhaps a little more often than others. And in my life time we very often sat down, the children in the family, and had a gathering of the family occasionally. And we laughed about how many cities we lived in as young children. And it became a ritual for -- to move from one city to another, which meant that we would have to make new acquaintances, and all of these things.
Change schools.
Yes, and all of these things associated with going into a new environment, new neighborhood, you see.
It's hard.

Very difficult. But it was a very important thing in my life which I think has had a lot to do with my being able to get along with my people in public life as a musician and entertainer, and of course most entertainers, I think musicians learn that you must get along with people in order to be appreciated, you know.
Now I must call you back because you were at that pot belly stove.

Yes. To this very day I do not understand why there's not a mark on my face from this because the stove -- like I said, it was absolutely, purely red hot, as you would have to bend steel. The same -- you remember those stoves.
Yes.
It was actually -- it got -- that stove sometimes got hot and was like a yellow color. What do they call that red, it was yellow. Yellow. You know?
Yes.

Now, what part of that stove -- I'm sure I didn't stick my face to that part, but I probably got it somewhere on the very hot part of the edge of the frame or something. But I know I hollered, I remember hollering. Now, these are the things I remember at the age of five, six years old, which is very interesting.
Yes.

And the next thing that I can remember what might be of interest is during the time when I was going to kindergarten, or perhaps the first grade, I may have been -- it might have been the kindergarten, what age do you go to kindergarten, first grade. Is it five or six?
Six, I think.
And right around the same period, I remember that I was very talented at art and drawing and

things of that sort. And I made a calendar which my mother kept for years and years and years and years, until I was almost a grown man she kept that calendar that I had made, of my real mother. My second mother kept that real calendar. With my picture on the calendar, you know, it's a calendar that I made. It's some sort of thing like that, you know.
Yes.

And I remember that, doing that, and it's about the only thing I can remember at that age. Which goes into another period of my childhood, later on as we said we moved quite frequently. During that time we lived in the state of Ohio, primarily including Springfield, where I was born, and then I had some relatives, an aunt, an uncle in Columbus. And this is where my mother died, my stepmother died, several years ago, in Columbus, Ohio. And I remember I went to school in Ohio during that time, when I was a young kid, and had the usual things happen to me like nails going through the foot running around barefooted, and so forth, and these little incidents.
And I think one time I was trying to hang onto a truck and I had a truck run over my toe. I think that's why I think ever now and then I -- now my toe nail comes off.
Oh, dear. You know, there's one thing I wanted to ask you. Where and when did your father get the training in the ministry, in the Methodist Church. That was
fairly considerable training, wasn't it?

Yes, it was. As I said, I don't know all these details, but as I said tonight I will talk to my sister and try to get some more actual facts of dates and so forth. Because I don't know. And I don't know whether they know that or not, but my father, as I said, primarily worked hard. He did many jobs. He's talked about how he had a horse and buggy. He did all kinds of things to make a living that was legal, to put himself through school. And in the process, as I said, he first was a school teacher, so that that primarily would be the fundamental background that you would need.
Yes.

And the other process would be just an idea of making it known that you wanted to become a minister, and then whatever the process of getting into the church was necessary he evidently did that. Because he was regarded as a very, very efficient minister.
When you were in school, this is in Columbus, did you make friends easily?

Well, this is -- I don't remember ever having any trouble making friends. I don't remember ever having a lot of good friends during that time. That's a little bit too early for me to remember. I -- my memory as far as remembering friends and things of that sort didn't start until I was 12 years old, precisely, when we were later on living in

another city, another state. But these periods of my early childhood, which I'm trying to remember as much as possible of, were at my mother's death and just after that. Which as I said I can't even remember the towns, all of the towns. I know we lived in Youngstown, Ohio, and during this same time I'd say the period between five and 12 I spent some time in one city where there was a terrible flood, and I remember it was very interesting to me as a boy to remember back how the people were going down the street in boats, and the water was up to the first floor of our house. And many of my father's important books and bibles and so forth got all wet and these things I remember because it's associated also with moving. Because these things I seem to recollect more than anything, and that is the moving, the consistent moving.

And my father had quite a library of books, encyclopedias and Christian bibles and material on teaching and literature. And of course I would always have to remember that we always had a piano in the front room, because my mother played, and everybody in the family played music.
Well, how old were you when you first started? When did you first start, with violin ?

Yes, that would come into the period when I was 12 years old. That's when I actually remember starting to play music, although I could play when I was five or six years old. I was always pluncking on the piano. And I
remember that. As I said, everybody in my family tells me how my mother used to hold me on her lap when she played.

But my official beginning of my knowledge of playing was at the age of 12, when I became interested in the violin. And there was a grown girl, I imagine she was perhaps 16 or 17 years old who played the violin in the church choir of my father's church. I believe that was Youngstown, Ohio, some city in Ohio, and I became interested in music through that source, the choir. I pumped the organ for the church, and in fact everybody in our family at some time or other had sang in the choir, and I eventually as a kid sang in the junior choir. I was always involved in the choir, and the music facilities of the church.

And -- but it was this interest that I heard from this violin played by this young girl that really got me interested in the violin, and I asked my father to buy a violin for me and he went and got me a violin. And I played it and I remember definitely I played it long enough to become a member of the citywide orchestra in Flint, Michigan.
Who instructed you?

I don't know the name but it was a city project at that time, which included young musicians from all of the schools, public schools in Flint, Michigan, and I don't know how, I was chosen. I remember I played second violin part. I don't think I was ever that good, but
evidently I must have been able to played in tune and read the notes to become a member of the citywide orchestra.
Well, violin isn't easy.

No, in fact that's why I stopped playing it. It was very difficult to really master the violin and I knew that and it gave me tone qualities. It was a life time job. Of course some people are gifted, and I think I must have been gifted to some degree. But I didn't have the mastery of fingering the instrument properly to completely get the sound that I thought was desirable. As I said, it must have been acceptable for the supervisor to choose me, you know. And I'm positive that I was able to play the notes, to read the notes properly and in tune.
And you probably had a good ear.
Oh --
You have a very good ear, haven't you?
There's no doubt. I think I have perfect pitch.
Have you really?

I've tested myself, in fact I do this as a game. I play a game with myself regularly, just no later than yesterday, benefit for T-Bone Walker at the musicians union here in Los Angeles, in Hollywood. I was testing my ability to do that, and I believe I have perfect pitch to the extent I can listen to anyone sing or play and
in a reasonable length of time I can tell which key they're in.
What key they're in. That's remarkable.
I can very often tell what key they've hit, what note, precisely what note. So I would have to say I have close to a perfect pitch. I'd like to test that out some time by some source.
Yes.
You know, with some --
They must have, in the music academy, they must have regular tests of a kind, haven't they?
Yes, they must -- I'm sure they do. I'd like to try it some time.
It would be very interesting. Very interesting. [PAUSE]
At this stage in your life, when you were 12, you were playing the violin, what else were you doing?

Well, Helen, this was when I was considering my life to really begin, as far as I'm concerned. And remembering things as much as possible. Of course I'd have to tell you I think all my life I've been affected with amnesia, and as I've progressed in my life time I think it became more predominant. I don't know what it is about my life but it seems as though once I get to concentrating on one thing I forget something that passed, unless it's something very important.

But this is when I began to remember things that developed in my life that started me to thinking on my own, and starting me to doing things and making decisions on my own. And I would have to say it starts with the playing of the violin because I became aware of what my interests were and I knew then that my first interest was music. This is what I think is very important in my whole career, is that I chose music. The first decision, the first choice that I made in my life as to what I wanted to do was music. And this is what I've stayed with, although other things have come into my life by necessity of economics, which I mentioned to you previously.

But I remember I chose to play the violin because I was interested in music. And in the process playing in the citywide orchestra gave me experience as a young boy, as a young black boy, if I might be so factual --
Specific.

Specific. Not only just a black boy but a light complected black boy, of a father who looked like a white man. My father did look like a white man, in fact he had more white look than anybody else. In fact it was during this time my father took me into a restaurant he'd been going in for several months, alone, and he took me into this restaurant one day, sat me down to eat, and the waiter came over and said, I'm sorry, the manager would like to see you.

And my father said, oh, yes okay. And the manager came over, and he asked me -- he asked my father, said what nationality are you. Well, my father being a very, very, very educated man and having plenty of experiences in dealing with people, I noticed -- and he mentioned before that he gave him a very simple answer. He said, I'm connected with the Negro race. At that time blacks were known as colored and Negro. And he said I'm connected with the Negro race.

And the guy said, I'm sorry, but we don't serve any Negroes in here. And this was because, even though my complexion was light, it was not white. And my hair was of the grade of black people. And my father went out naturally disgusted, and this is what started me off to thinking about not only economics but racial strifes of black people, which I think is very important. Or perhaps maybe you might not think it important.
I think it very important. I don't think there's anybody left today that doesn't, would you.

I want to be clear, as is become a famous saying now, I want to make it absolutely clear. But I want to give you as many facts as I can, and I think as I slowly go through this life of mine I think these things are important. And since this material is to be kept by officials who think it might be interesting and important, I think I should try to get in every aspect of my brain and my mind,
who is Sir. Charles Thompson. Right.
Who was born Charles Philip Walker Thompson.
How old were you when that happened, at the restaurant?
This was during the time, in this period -- I don't know exactly --
Around.
It was in this period, give or take before or after I was 12. But as I said it's like the center of my beginning, the age 12.
Did you say anything to your father or your father to you?

Oh, of course, of course. My father and I talked all the time. My father taught me from as early as I could remember, he taught me everything that I should know as much as possible that he could remember to tell me, and everything that happened he discussed it with me very manly-like. Because my father had interests in me and he wanted me to become a minister, and he trained me to be a minister at this time, as I said, which I'll tell you is a very important part of my life. He began to train me officially to be a minister, and I was very interested in it. I was dedicated.

I had intended to be a minister myself, and I was very interested. I was practicing, imitating my father, and we went to rituals, and we went to practice sessions in front of my family. Mainly my mother and father who would correct me and tutor me in this profession of the ministry.
That's interesting.
Quite fascinating.
Yes, very.

But any way, this incident that I told you about is very important in my life because it had to do with my total thinking, and I think that this is important because I think that the way my father thought, and the way I thought, and the way I acted, which I might inject was gentlemanly-like. My father was quite a fighter for rights, but he always had a gentlemanly-like manner of doing so. He never was a person to advocate violence, the fact of the matter is he was a non-violent man although as I told you before he was a strong individual who when he was a boy had been accosted by the law officials which were known as officers, because of many acts of fisticuffs, if you know what I mean.

And he always considered himself to be very proficient, and he taught me a few of those tricks, also. So as little men we considered ourselves to be quite capable of handling any -- four other men who weren't quite capable dealing with themselves properly.
That was very good.
So he was not only a minister, but he also was well trained in the mannerisms of what they now call the streets, if you know what I mean.
Yes.
And --
He wanted you to be equipped.

Well, yes. As I said his -- the person that had trained him, taught him that he had to defend himself, and this was before he became interested in the ministry, so just because he because he became a minister didn't mean that he was going to lose his ability to protect himself in cases of necessity.
Right.

So all of these things he passed on to me, as I said. We talked, and my father was very dedicated to me. Kept me with him all the time, tried to keep me out of trouble, because of the environments we were forced to live in, which were totally black, more or less, during the early stages of my life, it was necessary for him to keep me under his wing, see that I stayed out of trouble.

And there was a period of a year when my mother had died and between that time that my mother had died and the time he married, my father had to be father and mother. And of course with the help of the older sisters. And naturally

my being the youngest of the family, and the only one who was probably not capable of taking care of myself, he spent more time with me. And the fact of the matter is I used to be quite disturbed because I had to wait in the car for him to go around and take care of his business, which included going to see the afflicted sick, and going around the hospitals or what not, the daily chores that a minister has.

And in fact I'd like to pay a great tribute to him. My father was always active in doing things for the charity and for things in general of the neighborhood. And the fact of the matter is he was also very active in integrated meetings between white and black ministers. My father gave many sermons in white caucasian audiences, invited by minister of that congregation.
That was unusual in those days, wasn't it? Wasn't that about in the thirties?

You'd better believe it. And what I'm proud of is that my father did this at the invitation of the people who invited him, which was a feather in his cap. To me it's something I've always been proud of, my father was really and truly a wonderful and good man, and a great leader.
Especially if he didn't live many years in each town. I mean, it's all the more tribute, isn't it, if he was asked to speak in various churches? I mean he couldn't have been so well known?
Yes.
I mean, if you spend 10 years in a town, obviously various minister know one another well. But, I mean, that's very complimentary to him, isn't it.

As I said that's one of the things that always made me proud of my father, although we didn't see eye to eye on -- as I said, I was definitely not attracted to Christianity or the teachings of the bible as such, to be a minister. Because I changed my mind later. But I've always been very proud of my father because as you're saying, he couldn't have done all of this on his own. You can't -- you don't invite yourself to people, to people's houses for dinner, you know.
No.

And so it was definitely by invitation that my father did this, because he was -- it was very obvious that he was a leader of people and he was an adequate person for bringing about this closeness between the two races, black and white. And he didn't do it with a lot of loud talking. He did it by his actions of kindness and being a true minister, in keeping with the Methodist curriculum. And he was just -- and not only that but he was a likeable person. Up until the day he died he was laughing when he died.
We used to always -- he was the laugh of the party.

You know, he died, he was 97 years old, and right up until the time he died he was laughing, just having a ball, and having a good time, joking and carrying on. He was that kind of person. Even though he was strict, you had to love him because you knew that he was being strict because he wanted you to be right, you know, and he insisted that you were right. But in the process, after this was over, he was a very jolly, in fact he was almost like a comedian, you know. He could do so many things also. I mean I was always astounded at the many things my father could do. He could even juggle, he could juggle balls. And you know, you'd think a minister would be a guy, especially in the --
Sober sides.

Yes. Particularly my father, because in the church he was definitely right down the middle. He didn't vary, everything had to be according to the way it was. And you would think he couldn't do anything else. My father was so talented it was unbelievable, you know, so many things he could do. And of course that's why he made such a good teacher, because he understood people, he understood what made people tick, and he understood the true values of the bible, you know.
Yes.
Even though he made his sermons in

the light of the information in the bible, the scriptures. He had a way of bringing it about in what he called parables, so that people could see the reason for these things, because anyone that reads the bible would have to understand that the bible's written B.C., way back there before Christ. I mean, how can you possibly understand all these words that have been [jungled] around -- jumbled around or, you know --
Right.
It's very difficult to accept the bible in the words that they're written.
Yes, that's true.
And for these things --
And relating to those times, and then to try to relate it to these times.
That's right.
Right.
So in the process -- what I'm saying is that's why I was very close to my father.
Yes.
He taught me to drive an automobile when I was 12 years old.
Did he?
And everything as he told me I remembered as he told me. The good things he taught and he tried to teach me the good things. Unfortunately, I'd have to admit

that I haven't adhered to all of the things he taught me, but it has given me, I think, a background in my mind that has been very instrumental in perhaps my survival in many hard conditions that I've experienced as a travelling jazz musician. And for this I'm very thankful, you know?
Yes, that's wonderful. Do you think that you were particularly dear to him in that perhaps your elder brother was in some way a disappointment to him?

Oh, I don't think my brother was -- I think my father was beyond disappointment. That's another thing about him. Of course you never knew what he was thinking, that's another thing. He was able to hide his emotions very well as a minister. But I'm sure it disturbed him because naturally I know as a man myself, I think the most disturbing thing that can happen to a father is to have anything happen to a son. Because it's a man's ambition to have a son that he can raise in his own image or pass something on to him that can make him an improvement on his own image.
Yes.
And for that reason I'm sure he was very disappointed about my older brother. But as I said most of these things were kept from me, from the whole family.
Yes.
For some reason or other, which I intend to find out shortly.
We'll get to that shortly.
Yes. I hope before this interview is over maybe I might be able to call [ ] and find out what happened.
Shed some light on that mystery. Well, tell me. You said that there were other interests. What about athletics at that age?

Well, I -- for some reason or other that's why I play so much importance on age 12 in my life. It's because this was when I started everything. Athletics and everything. All of a sudden I became a man, you might say, at the age of 12, because I was able to decide for myself getting back to the fisticuffs. All right, my father had taught me so many things, mental things and spiritual things, and now at the age 12 I became aware of myself as a physical man, and where I had to also protect myself, which is a very important thing when you move around from city to city, from environment to environment, where you are predominantly more or less in the what you call now the ghetto era -- area, you know.

Of course I might embellish on this too, because my father for some reason or other was always able to have some sort of relationship where during the course of my childhood we lived in semi-integrated neighborhoods. Now, this is way back in those days, you know. We've got to be talking
Right.
You know. And I remember -- many times we lived in what you call a semi-integrated area, where I associated with many white people. And this was unusual then, you know.
Yes.

But however, naturally, we were more or less predominantly in black neighborhoods, but they were always nice neighborhoods and of course my father and mother being cultured people, our home was as clean and nice as the next person's, you know. But it was this time that I became aware of my athletic ability because there were times I had to protect myself as a boy. You know, when you carry a violin under your arm, and you're not too big -- you know, I was not a great specimen of Charles Atlas type, you know, and fact of the matter is I was always sorry that I didn't weigh about 100 pounds more, you know. I think I could have even made a little more noise in the new neighborhoods.

But many times when I'd come down the street with my violin, many of the boys would challenge me, you know, I mean want to take my violin away from me. Well, now everything they would say to me would be, I could take. They'd call me names or whatever or not, but when they grabbed that violin boy, they were in trouble.
You -- I guess you just felt so strongly about it that you were able to assert yourself.

Listen, when they put their hands on that violin, that was it. I put the violin down and picked up a brick. But this was very -- I didn't have any -- I remember -- I didn't have what you call violent incidents, but there were -- you know, as little boys are, I was very fortunate, I think, by the training of my father, of what to say and how to walk away from fights when necessary and when possible. The combination of those things, I think, made it -- so I don't remember ever having any real violent fights or anything like that. But I remember several incidents where I had to assert myself, and it paid off.

I had a bicycle during this time, my father had bought me wagons, and all the things that boys should have, skates and things. And I'd have these scuffles in new neighborhoods, you know, they'd come in there and they'd think you're a minister's son and you're a little bit on the weak side, and they'd try to take your bicycle. In fact I had some larger boys who did take my bicycle once and my father had to go get it for me. This is a -- understandable, particularly in the days where you could be a man and walk down the street and some kids will take your bicycle now.
That's quite. But what about sport, were you playing sport at school?
Yes, as I said, this is how I became

interested in sports, more or less, I guess through that facility. And naturally in the gym of the public schools, as I said. As early as this time we were living then in Colorado Springs, Colorado, and this was an integrated school. Now, I can remember some incidents of that integrated school where one time I had some problems with one of the teachers who I at that age thought was a little bit biased about race. And I went home and told my father about it, he came to school, and I believe he sort of had the same feelings.

Because I never was a person to lie to my father, that's one thing I remember. I never was a person to lie. I'd stretch a story a little bit when it came to coming home late, to keep from getting chastised about that, but things of that sort I never lied about. But it was during this time that I started into athletics on the school team, you know, in gymnastic classes. I played basketball as a young boy, 12 years old, I was very small but I participated. And I got into track, and it was there that I learned my ability and I had some ability. I played ball, played all the sports that you play, you know.
And I also became interested in golf.
That early?
At that early age I became interested in golf, which has actually been I'd say one of the greatest physical aspects of my life, and things that has perhaps kept
me a little more healthy than I would have been had I not been interested in golf.
Yes.

It was during this time there was a combination of need to enhance the bankroll, you know, my father gave me things that I needed, nice clothes, and in return I had to be sure and take care of them. So I didn't have an abundance of clothes, but I had nice clothes for church and for outings and I had my school clothes and I had my play clothes. But I was becoming a man, as I said, in my visions, in my actions, and I realize that my father didn't have enough money to give me everything I wanted.

So I knew that I had to find a way to get it, and try to find a legal method to get this money. And I didn't want to be bad, I didn't want to be a hoodlum, I mean I found, I mean, I wasn't very efficient at stealing milk bottles like the rest of the guys because I didn't feel that that was a very, very complimentary to my father as a minister, should I get caught.
Yeah.

And this fear made me seek a legal means of getting a little extra money for myself. And would you believe it, at the age of 12 years old I tried getting a job as a dishwasher? And it wasn't one day before I found out that this was not for me because first of all my mother

taught me to be very immaculate and clean, and I was always very particular about clothes, and my hands were very sensitive. And just the thought of going into that nasty kitchen with those dishes, it just terminated my desire to be a dishwasher. You know?
Yes, I know that.
You know what I mean?
Yes.

I could have taken all this, perhaps, because, you know, to earn the money, and I was becoming interested in girls even. I wanted to take a girl to the show, or buy her a box of candy, I wanted this money badly, and I would have properly done anything within reason, but it was the continuation of dishes that came into the kitchen. As soon as I get finished with one batch I'd say, oh, I'm finished, now here comes another batch. Pow. And I think I lasted -- I don't remember whether I lasted a whole day, and the guy paid me off at the end of that day, or before the day started, or the next day, but I know I didn't last very long at that, you know.
I do.
So in the process I heard that some of the young boys was making money caddying, you know.
Yes.
And so I said, well maybe that's

something interesting because -- now up to this time we played golf in a field that was right across the street from my house, and my house was on a deadend street in Colorado Springs, where out of my window where I got -- you know, slept every night and went to school every day, to the public schools, right in that window I could see Pikes Peak all year around, and there was snow on top of that mountain which was the most fascinating sight.
(Inaudible).

Now, I would have to say it was a combination of this that led me up into those mountains where it was Broadmoor, Colorado, where they had a country club. And one of the most famous golf pros in the history of golf, whose name incidently was the same as mine with the exception of the spelling -- his name was Jimmy Thomson, he spelled his T-h-o-m-s-o-n, I believe he was Irish. And would you believe it, there's supposed to be Irish in my family.
Really?
Yes.
You never know, would you?
That's interesting, isn't it?
Right.
But there was a field across from my house, you know, and we played golf with one club, all of the kids in the neighborhood. I was 12, there was guys 15, 16, my

best friend was a football player. He was older than me but he was almost in my same class because he wasn't too bright. I won't call his name right now. But he was a football star, you know, and he was very good. He was the star of the team.

We all lived in this neighborhood, you know, and we played golf. We dug holes at each end of this lot, which was about a quarter of a block long. About a shot for a wedge, a nine iron. Right? Anyone who knows anything about golf knows that's around anywhere from 90 to 120 yards. Perhaps the lot could have been -- I'd say at the most 150 yards.
Yes.

We played with one club, and would you believe it that these kids that I'm talking about, including myself, when we played that one hole from one end to the other -- it was two holes, one end -- anyone who had over three would have to be a loser. Now, just imagine kids playing golf with one club, and I'm sure it was a nine iron, and we went from one end of that club playing for match sticks, and very often we had two's and one's a couple times, a few times a guy would have a one, very rarely, but we'd always have three's on that hole, more or less. Every now and then two, which is known as a birdie, on par three hole. And this is how I started playing golf.
So I had the interest in playing golf, plus some-

thing about that mountain intrigued me because one day I had stolen my father's car, while he was giving a sermon at a caucasian church, and I and some other fellas went to the church and got the car and took it for a ride and got caught on the railroad tracks in those mountains going up to Broadmoor, Colorado, and we didn't get back in time.

To show you what kind of man my father was, when we came back, the church was out and they were all standing out there, all this big congregation. The minister's car's been stolen. They're all out there, just after the sermon's over. And we took the car and we left the car out there and ran, you know. You know my father told me later on, he never chastized anybody, never mentioned it, but he told me many years later that he knew it was me that got that car. But he wouldn't allow them to call the police because he knew it was me. He felt -- he was almost sure, because I had a key, see, I had a key made. He didn't know at the time, but I had -- while he was asleep one time --as you can see I must have been very mischievous when I was 12, so that accounts for all --
You were A proper boy.
That accounts for all my bad behaving -- what do you call it, all of my misbehavior.
Misbehavior, yes.
During my manly years.
He never said a word to you about it?
Not until years later, many years later he told me he knew that --
Did you suspect he knew?
I never knew because my father was the type of man, you never knew what to think about him, you never knew -- you felt that he knew everything.
Yes.

And he had those eyes, you know, those kind of eyes, those blueish-green eyes, that, you know, you can't tell what's coming out of eyes of an owl. But it was another one of those kindly gestures of my father. He was, as I said, a very stern man, a very, very -- you know, very stern, but he was very understanding and he never chastized me about that. He mentioned it to me a couple of times, asked me if I stole that car. I never told him the truth. You know?
Well, what's happened though up there. You say there was a --
(Tape 2)
You said that was important to you, going up there. What did happen then?

Well, there was many things that happened that fascinated me in those mountains which they call Pikes Peak. The combination of just all of these stories that I'd heard about it, and this particular incident, going half way up the mountain or a certain part of that moun-
tain. You know, they used to have auto races up that mountain. It was a very historic mountain, Pikes Peak. You've probably heard of it, right?
I've heard of it.

So this was all significant, and it had a lot to do with my visions and so forth, plus the fact that Broadmoor, Colorado was up that mountain where this golf course was. And that's where I became interested in golf, which helped to round out my athletic ambitions, you know. Actually I might say that I was a little bit small for the sports. To really be a top star. I was too small to play football, of course, really play and compete. I did. Naturally when you're children you compete in all these things because size is not that important then. But later on it becomes important. In basketball you must be tall, and agile. And in football you must be heavy and rough. And in baseball must be able to face the fast ball, of a left handed pitcher throwing a curve at your head that winds up over the plate. Do you know anything about that?
A little.

That's pretty hard to deal with. And I might say that incidentally I had an incident happen to me during that period of early childhood when the family was playing ball, and another one of my sisters, Louise -- we were playing ball and I was catching, and on her back swing she
hit me in the mouth with the bat. So if I show any signs of being slightly afflicted with insanity, of some sort, you can understand I've had several instances -- incidents that happened to cause it.

Also, in Chicago, one of the many places where my father was minister, I remember sliding down a hill on a sled and hitting a boulder with my head, stopping the sled and me and everything with the boulder in my head, you know.
That didn't help.
I think that the thorough examination of my brain might bring some revelations of importance.
Well, you have to enlighten me as to what did you eventually develop a connection with the golf and with the Broadmoor, or where did you go caddy-carrying?
I proceeded immediately to go to those hills, to get a job as a caddy.
You did.

And I never will forget the first day I went there, because of my size, I was a little small, they threw me in the lake. There was a lake there, around the club house and the caddy shack, in that area. They threw me in that lake, clothes and all, shoes and everything, all the rest of the caddys, because I was so little. And they just took me bodily and threw me out in that lake, you know. And I think that this perhaps was maybe one of my tests of durability
and everything.
Yes. Endurance.

Yes. Because -- and I think that's what they used it for in those days. You know, during that period, you know, it was a hard time -- you know, people were -- the world was very cultured in the christian world and so forth, in the highly cultured world, but there was a lot of rough experiences in the lower level of things in life, you know, like common people and so forth. And that particular job, they didn't need any caddys, and they wanted to discourage young people or guys who didn't know anything about golf, or I guess in some senses it was a test of your ability to take it.
Yes.

And this I suppose I guess to discourage you, which as I remember it did finally discourage me because I didn't feel that that was the thing for me, and I think they probably eventually made me decide more to be a musician. Some of these experiences of that sort.
Yes.

Because I didn't feel like I wanted to take all these things, and then at that time the pay was so bad, it was so small it wasn't even funny. They paid you 75 cents for nine holes, to carry those big, heavy bags around, and $1.50 for nine. And I remember, I think that --
For 18.
Right.

And as I remember it, I never passed a stage of chasing shagging balls, in other words that means you go out in the fairway and let the pro hit balls, or he's teaching somebody, and you pick up the balls. Well, now that's very dangerous. For one thing you're looking in the sun, you can't see the balls, and if you miss catching the ball too fast he's going to make some remarks, very unkindly remarks, calling you all kinds of names which I don't want to repeat on this tape.
No.
But that sort of thing, very, very tough job, you know. And for a kid that age, I just couldn't take it, and I didn't have to do this.
No.
For a living, so I was rather discouraged with that type of thing.
Yes.
But, it created my interests in golf and also made me see enough of this perfect form and talent of Jimmy Thompson, the pro, to be able to simulate it.
Is that right? How much did you see him then?
(dragged?)
Well, I shared balls for him.
How long?
Oh, I don't know. The short period of time that I was out there. I don't know how long it was.
Was it a week or two?
I don't know. It could have been a week or two.
A time, a little time.
Yes, you know. Long enough to remember.
And you spotted what he was doing.
I saw all what was the fundamentals of a golf swing, and I saw --
(Inaudible).

Well, incidentally, Jimmy Thomson was the first long ball hitter of note in professional golf. This is quite significant, because today the game has come around in 1975, a game of long ball hitters dominating the game, such as the likes of Jack Nicklaus, who has proven that a man, a heavy weight who has finesse and timing and feeling is better than any small man, because he hits the ball so far. But at that time Jimmy Thomson was considered to be something of a freak of nature because he could hit the ball so far, and he just gave clinics of hitting a ball.
I remember in fact later on going to see some of his
Yes.

And it's quite coincidental that many years later when I came to California for a short time, during one of my periods when I was travelling back to California, because I liked to be where it was warm, and I had some engagements in California, and I got experience of seeing him play in some of the PGA sponsored tournaments, and I think he was perhaps in his sixties or something like that, or a very old man, and he still played a very, very good game of golf, highly competitive and in the seventies.
Remarkable (Inaudible).
Yes, that same man that I caddied for.
Isn't that something.
Yes.
Quite how wonderful.

So that's where my athletic participation you might say started. I think my whole awareness of being a person and making some decisions for myself starting during this same time of the age 12, and I began playing the violin, and participating in sports, realizing that I did have some ability in this field. But however, the irony of it, and I think the significant part of this part of my conversation is that how even knowing of this athletic ability, and also
realizing the limitations of being successful, I chose music, and it became my final decision even though I went from that to other things in the course of my schooling during this period.
Yes.

I also took up in school, which I think is quite important, and it's a wonderful thing for people in school, is that in the schools they had these classes in woodwork, sheet metal, and auto mechanics.
Yes.
And I was fortunate enough to be in those classes, as I said, which was furnished by the public schools.
In all three of them?

In all three of them. And I showed some signs of having talent in those three things. I had another article that I made that my second mother kept, which was a ship. It was a ship I made out of wood. You know, imitation of the sailboats.
Yes, sailing ships.
Sail boats, the old sailing boats.
Yes.
And I had a sail boat that I made out of wood that my mother kept, and some lamps that I made in the woodwork class. I liked it and I still like it. To me
it's a great hobby.
Creative.
Yes. That's right. You might say that these were creative abilities that I was interested -- I was always interested in the arts.
Yes.

And I liked it, but I guess music you might say was the dominant one because it probably was the easiest one for me to pursue, because having an instrument I could pursue that field and being around music in the church, and other sources, radio. And in fact it was this time that I started hearing great jazz music, that began to penetrate my ear.
Who did you hear?

At that time I remember hearing the orchestras -- it possibly was people like Rudy Vallee, I remember specifically remember hearing Rudy Vallee, and of course Bing Crosby. And at that time the Mills Brothers were very, very, very important figures in the world of entertainment.
I remember.
And to this very day they have always been gentlemen and they have been a guiding line for better entertainers.
They have a beautiful sound.

Beautiful sound, beautiful talent, and just absolutely impeccable and well disciplined. And I think that they perhaps have been -- I would say to me they've been the most outstanding, all black group of entertainers that I've ever seen in my life.
I don't think any group topped them.

I don't think that they could be topped. I think they're the sort of people, the kind of things that can't be taught. There are some things that are just best, and you can only match that. And I think that's what the Mills Brothers represented to me. And I would have to truthfully say that the things that I have tried to do in the line of better morals and setting examples for others have been things that I've admired in the Mills Brothers. And it started when I was living in Colorado Springs, Colorado at the age of 12.
Well, you know, at that time you must have heard also Duke Ellington.
Well, I didn't hear Duke -- I heard Duke Ellington a little after that, you know.
Yes.
You know, as I said, I was telling you the people --
Of course you were out west.
I was telling you people who were
significant --
Yes.
That's why I say it's important that I bring it in order --
Yes, it is important.
Being in a Christian atmosphere, naturally the music that came in off of our radio was limited.
Yes.

Because most of the things that we were allowed to hear were Christian music, you know, as I said, my father was always active, not only in the field of ministry but the field of entertainment. When you speak of choirs and singing and the different entertainment that the church had, and this exchanging of clientele between the blacks and the whites. My father would take his choir to sing at the choirs of the caucasian audiences, and vice versa. This was going into effect during these days.
Yes.

This was perhaps during that period -- I would have to say during that period there perhaps was a surge of efforts on many people to bring together the goodness of people in both races, which I'm sure had a lot to do with our present society.
Yes.
You know.
Coming -- it came from the good sources.

Yes. The fact of the matter is I really think that in my way of thinking I think that the style and method of those people was more effective than the style that has become effective lately through the violence that has caused a lot of changes. Although I don't consider myself to be that well versed and educated in the technical sources of why's and, you know, so forth. But as a common observer of what has happened through the history of our nation, and we have to all realize that there's no question that America is no doubt the greatest nation on earth at this time. And if anyone wants to be controversial about it, I might say one of them. But it's my opinion that America is the greatest country in the world.

And I would have to include that in any statements that I make here or after, because I've been all over the world. I'm fortunate. I haven't covered the whole world, but I have been lucky enough to travel to many remote spots, and many places, and I've compared societies. And I'm sure that America will go down in history as perhaps being comparable to the Roman days when they were ruling the world. You know what I mean?
Yes.
But getting back -- we were at the
point of this golf and --
What you were listening to.
Yes, the music that I was listening to.
I wanted to bring it in chronological order.
of course you must.
Yes (inaudible)
As to how I heard this.
It had an effect on you.
Yes.
Because you heard it.

What I was trying to say primarily, the music that I was attracted to first had to be naturally the classical music and the cultured music that was coming in over the airways at that time. And of course the better singers. Like I said it started out with -- well, like I said, Rudy Vallee Rudy Vallee and Bing Crosby.
Yes.
These are people who stand out in my mind as the music that I heard. And the Mills Brothers, you see.
Right.

And of course later on came Jack Benny to throw in the [jester gesture.] I don't remember when he started, it seems as though he's been going as long as I can remember too. And I think he was 39 then.
Yes.
So that's my age now, I'm 39.
Then you -- but you spoke specifically of jazz. Now when you first have been exposed to jazz? I mean you were exposed to it through the Mills Brothers, certainly, but where else?
Well, I didn't consider the Mills Brothers to be exactly jazz, although -- yes, I would have to consider in the field of jazz, yes. But now --
Their phrasings.

Yes. But in that order, as I said, my musical ear was trained from the classical music that I'd played in the citywide orchestra. Now, you must remember that I started out as a classical violinist, and I didn't study the piano formally as a classical pianist. I studied the piano by way of my mother teaching me the fundamentals, and I had a few lessons to teach me the fingerings. And I remember at that time I had been through the first three books of the Williams Piano Book, which included the Minuet in G, the last classical piece I remember being interested in or disgusted with because of the technicalities of the fingering.
Yes.

And the teacher hit my hands with a ruler to make me realize that I didn't have them in the proper position, and my rebellion against being feminine type, as I said, because I was an athlete, you see, it didn't fit

me exactly. I was discouraged along the lines of classical music. As I said, along with the fact that many of these ruffians used to grab the violin and there was always the danger of it getting destroyed, or my being called a sissy.

So I think maybe these things had something to do with my getting away from the classical sounds as well as the environment that I lived in, particularly an all black congregation at the church where they were singing spiritual music, and I might add that this is a good point to talk about the types of music that I became interested in, which go into even the present day music of 1975. At that early age there was a classification of even black music, which was considered to be somewhat cultured and non-cultured.

And it was even divided, if I might say, into classifications of demonenations of churches. For instance as I said the Methodist church actually was not really totally accepted among black people because of the rigid cultured requirements.
Yes.
And I believe --
Not enough flexibility.

Right. And at that time quite a number of blacks was associated with the Baptist church. And they were noted for more or less this rhythmic expression of what is now known as soul music, you know. But they were
known for their clapping and chanting, you know. Rather the /methodist church concentrated on the hymns, choir, hymns which was considered to be more cultured, if I might use the word, continually.
Right.

You know? And so there again you have a discipline of music that I was hearing, which was associated with classical music, and of course my mother was appreciative of classical music. And the music that I heard on the radio naturally had to be music that was fitting -- befitting of the atmosphere in our home. It was a very serene atmosphere. So I heard the classical music, and I remember hearing Paul Whiteman, see.
Yes.
So all this joins up with my later interest in jazz. The Mills Brothers I didn't consider to be completely jazz. They were high class entertainers.
Yes.
And I remember they used to imitate the horns.
I remember.
(Imitation of the Mills Brothers) And the guy would (Imitation).
Yes, and the fella with the (inaudible).
Right. And of course I did [it] and

now thinking about this, this is actually when I started molding my entertaining personality, and I'm getting away from gradually being a minister because I don't seem to fit in that environment as a minister, and I'm beginning to rebel against this priestly image, you see. The combination of my interest in sports, and participating with physical combat, and all of these things, plus -- and I hate to inject this--but the violent sources of racial conflict.
Yes.

All these things had to do with changing my viewpoints about music, and my listening ear, and my rebellion against this atmosphere that I was growing up in. In other words at 12 years old I realized that I was growing up in a dual atmosphere, one that my father required me to be a saintly gentleman, and immediately when I would go -- on my way to school I'd find out that I was not living in that world of Jesus Christ, but a world of reality where there was physical strife and conflict, you know.
Yes,yes.
So in other words this had to do with my choice of music at that age, that we were talking about. As I said, going up in those hills and casting, the decisions and all that.
Yes.
So in other words my golf career
ended rather suddenly too and I went back to playing the piano this time.
Oh, you went back to piano.

Yes. I realized that the violin was a little too feminine for me. I think that's what you might say would be the explanation of it, you know, as I grew into manhood early. Because all of my friends were always larger boys, and to this day most of my friends are heavy weights. Isn't that funny?
It is funny.
I'm a bantam weight, and all of my best friends have been heavy weights.
Isn't that funny.

Extremely heavy weights, and we have tussled -- I've actually tussled with heavy weights, and we have a thing together that seems to be an understanding. This is something I'd have to go into. I guess it would be some discussion for somebody in the field of psychiatry.
Yes, they would know what's in the back of all that.
Why does a big man take to me, why does a little man meet such a big man.
Yes, that's funny right.
But all my friends are heavy weights, but I think it's this physical contact that I've had, perhaps

in my early life, as an athlete, that has brought this about. I used to play football until I got the wind knocked out of me and I realized that this wasn't for me. My father was watching me too, incidentally. He tried to help me do anything I wanted to do.
That's wonderful.

Right up until the time I left home. And he didn't approve of that, but I'll tell you about that later when we get into that at a later time of my life when I finally left home, left school. But I want to try to cover everything I can.

Yes. I want you to tell me when you turned to piano then were you just playing -- you went through those three first books -- but when did you first get away from the strict discipline of classicism on the piano.

Well, much later. I didn't -- in fact I didn't get away from that until I finally decided to leave home, and I did this in a legal manner by joining the branch of the army, peace time army then, which was known as Civilian Conservation Corps, which was several years later when I was at the age -- oh, that would be at least five years later.
So you never played jazz piano until you were 17 or 18.
Actually I didn't play what you might

say jazz piano per se, but however I said because of the environment that I was in, these the people around me, when I would go to peoples' houses, naturally, and I didn't include in my information awhile ago -- I said that I started listening to these other musicians. There was also Fats Waller, you see.
Right.
And I had heard Fats Waller, so naturally --
On records you've heard him or did you (inaudible) on the air?

Yes, on records. At this time everything I heard was either on records or by means of record player, that someone else had in their homes when I visited their homes. And naturally, all the -- it's a funny thing. People like to think of ministers' children as models, and in fact they always say that ministers' children are the worst people in the neighborhood. That is now I'm telling you about the black commentations. Is that the right word?
Yes, that it is.

It was always commonly accepted that the minister's children were the worst people in the neighborhood, which was not really true. It was just that everyone expected that the minister's children to be models.
Yes.

But in my association with the rest of the sinners, I picked up some of the ways of the sinners. Which I couldn't carry home with me, but when I was away from home, in their houses, I had to be like they were to be friends with them, so I picked up some of their not so saintly ways.
Right.
Which included playing jazz music on the side when my father didn't know what I was doing.
Right.
You see?
Yes.

So it was that early age that I picked up naturally these jazz sounds, and it was first Fat Waller Whiler who I heard play, and he was -- since I've read later, the story of his life, which I think it's called Handful of Keys.
Yes.

I read that book recently. And from all indications, what I heard then and what I later found out from hearing him later, and from what I read, there's no doubt in my mind that Fat Waller Whiler was perhaps the greatest piano genius jazz has ever known.
Really?
That's right.

Now, I'd have to -- I've always been an admirer -- my number one pianist in the jazz field is Art Tatum. Because of his talent. But I'd have to put them together, you know, one and two are together as a dead-heat.
Yes. One and one.

Because Fats Waller no doubt had the master for style, and he was -- the man was just creative and not only that but he had enough laughter about him to make people listen to his playing. But however many people don't know how talented he was.
And he had that sense of time, rhythm and everything that was infallable sense of rhythm.
Yes. And the thing I think made him more popular than Art Tatum was he was louder. That's the thing that made him -- Fats Waller what he was.
Yes.

He was a talented man, loud. He was a loud, talented man, because -- well, he was a big man, and he talked loud and he laughed loud and he played loud, and he played so loud that he could drown out the drums. That's pretty loud.
Yes, that's right.
But it was good music, so -- in fact Fats Waller is the only person I've ever heard in my life who played loud who could make me appreciate it. Of course Louie
Armstrong had the same quality, you might say.
Yes.
But usually a pianist, you don't want to hear him play loud.
No.
But Fats Waller could play a piano loud but pretty. And good.
That's remarkable.

Yes, it is, and unusual. So with -- it was through him that I really got interested in the piano, to really want to play it. I knew that the violin was not for me, and I might also add while I'm talking about this, it's very important. My initial reason for discarding the violin, and this is in my mind, in my brain as the initial reason was -- and believe you me this is the truth -- it was my being able to see how limited the field of violin would be for me as a black man. As I said, at the age of 12 years old I became grown in my thinking, you see.
Yeah. And you could look ahead.

Already I could see that I was going to be very limited as to how far I could get as a violinist. So I had to choose another instrument, and fortunate for me I'd had some lessons on the piano, and with the knowledge of the violin, reading the notes -- of course we had reading in school, incidentally, which I had forgot to discuss with you.
In all of my public school training we had sight reading, vocal instructions.
You had very good schooling, didn't you?

I was very -- as I told you, I -- my -- I give my father credit for giving everyone in my family an opportunity to educate themselves as far as they wanted to go. I could have gone to college, but I felt that it would be a little bit too much of a burden on my father, and as I said I became worldly inclined and I wanted to get out from under this highly religious regimentation, the combination of those things maybe, to decide for myself. But I had the best of schooling that could be gotten as a black man or a black child. And I was raised in a highly intellectual background which has a lot to do, I think, with my style and my interpretations.
Yes. Formed the man, didn't it?
Yes. So I don't know, I perhaps think that that would probably bring me up to a further period in my life, which I think we could talk about now.
What period? When you were 16 and 17 you mean?
Yes, going up into that period, which when I started going with the girls --
