I was just going to say you started to say you'd like to --
Yes, this was next.
-- take the occasional girl out.

Yes, you see, all of this has to do with my learning to decide for myself or becoming -- wanting to decide for myself. I became interested in girls, I remember my first little girl friend that I decided I wanted to take out to the show. And I was a little bashful and so forth, you know. One of those things in your life that everybody goes through during the same time.
Yes.
And I didn't feel that I was too successful at this, and I don't know, I think you might say in that period I maybe elected to sort of be a loner, because of all of this atmosphere, this --
Conflict.

Conflict of interest. Wanting to be congenial and accepted by the outer public, but yet being sheltered and disciplined at home; you see, this was a conflict in my life, you see. And it was hard for me to deal with that as a child, see, because even the people, when they came to church they would mind their manners and everything, but most people when they went to church in those days, they'd come into church and as soon as they'd leave the church they'd take off their tie and take off their shoes, and sit down with a beer or some scotch and soda, or a home brew, or
corn liquor, whatever. And forget about all that.
But you see, I was under this all the time, you see.
Yes.
And so this conflict was there, and I didn't have too much ambition to try things like other people. I think perhaps I was somewhat discouraged, you might say, because it was like --
You were handicapped.

Right, it was a handicap for me. Not -- in other words I just -- I think I had a feeling of not being wanted, or not being accepted in either side. Not wanting to be as my father wanted me to be, and not knowing whether I was wanted on the other side. See. But as I grew up -- now, because of this, because of the environment, of people around me, as I said, my father would have a church on one corner in many instances, and on the next corner or the opposite corner there probably could be a house of ill repute.
Yes.
Or a gambling establishment. You know?
Yes.
Or a pool hall.
Yes.
So I was thrown in to this environment at an early age, with this conflict of interest, and plus as I said before when I started out about the economical
pressure. You see, economics makes a person make decisions early in life that they might not normally make otherwise.
No.
This need for --
That's right.
-- of material things, and money.
And so it makes it very easy to be enticed to get involved in some things that are not looked up as to be the better fields of endeavor.
Right.
Like for instance playing pool, you know.
Did you play pool?
I played pool at an early age that's what I'm saying. You see, I got thrown into that, you automatically get thrown into that.
Yes. Were you good?

Well, some of the people that I took money from seemed to think I was. I didn't -- I never considered myself to be a vicious competitor, but I never was a good loser. And I say this by saying that I never wanted to lose, and I would do everything in my power, that was legal, not to lose. And getting back, not trying to be boastful, or not trying to -- I'm being honest. As I said I still had this influence from my father, and I never considered myself suc-

cessful at cheating. And all these things I did, like playing pool, whatever, I always wanted to win with honor. And I've been in some situations where I've had a chance to cheat or steal, and many of my teachers or cohorts were expert thieves and you know, like the hand is quicker than the eye type. And I learned a lot of those tricks, but I used them only to protect myself. And I've always used that theory. Whether it's good or bad, I don't know, but I feel good about it, you know, that even then I always tried to use a way of honor, you know.
Yes. You knew you ought to be honest.
Well, I was taught that way, you know, let's put it that way.
That's right.

And I believe that and I still believe it, and no matter what happens it seems to be evident I think that the right way is usually the best way. There's a friend of mine here in Los Angeles by the name of Paul Howard. He was the secretary of the black musician's union, the old one, 767, which I was a member when I came to California years ago, and I went over to the integrated union, local 47. But he used to have a saying, that I never forgot. He said, if you never lie you never have to remember anything.
Very good.
Which I think is a good example of

what I'm talking about. You know, although, you know, we all know that our conscience can bother us. But I think it's very evident today that the conscience won't stop us. You know, if that were the case we wouldn't have so many millionaires, if consciences were that bad, you know, they would kill us.
That's right, yes.

But the conscience does have something to do with our looks and our personality, and I like to feel that I have at least some normal, happy reactions and pleasant reactions because of the fact I feel that maybe I didn't use some of those tactics that went on.
And you don't have to carry a burden of guilt.
Well, yes.
Which is something.
As I said, it's debatable. I think maybe perhaps now that I'm at my age now, I think perhaps I might be able to carry those burdens a little easier. You know?
Well, you'll have to try and find out.

Well, I don't know, it might be a little late for that, but I'll say one thing. I found out from playing jazz music, and I've watched other musicians because being an arranger and composer of music I have studied personalities, because in order to compose music and

write music, you have to know something about people. And expressions, moods. And I have noticed in my playing and other peoples' playing, you know, if you're not happy you can't express good music. I mean, you can only express music that you feel and it's usually if you feel bad you're going to play bad, or it's going to sound bad.

And I don't want to get into that too deep right now but it has to do with a style of music, or the popularity of music at a time. What people listen to has to do with what they believe and what they think. And you know, like if you think pretty you play pretty, you see.
Yeah.
And no matter how mean you may be, at the time you're playing you have to think -- if you're going to play pretty you have to think pretty.
Yes.
Or with love.
You can't be in an evil mood --
Right.
-- and have it come out pretty.

Right. Even if you're expressing the evil part of the blues, of which there are some evil parts of blues, you have to be able to express it with a mirth. That's why the great exponents of the blues, like T-Bone Walker and others are able to captivate audiences. It's because they can show
the mirth, the and comedy of the sadness of the blues. You see?
Very nice.
And I think right here I should stop for a minute to get my breath.
I do too. I think it's wonderful, what we've done.
[PAUSE]
So we'll just go to this where I say -- I'm talking about when I say that how good you sound, and you say that people always did tell you how good you sound. Go from there.

Well, that's a compliment, and as I was telling you before we turned the tape on, we were discussing this point of music sounding good. And you said that you'd like to hear me play. What I was saying was, which is significant in this period of my life, starting from 12 years old, it seems as though as long as I can remember, people have always told me how good I sound, you know. And as I said, this has naturally been inspirational to me but it has never dawned on me as being a fact, because of my lack of knowledge and desire to study to better myself. And realizing that those who are much better than me.

So I never really realized how good I was, or what I was doing until recently. Now, I would say this, in other words to try to clarify this, I still don't feel I'm good enough, or there's much I want to learn. But I now seem to

realize that there is something in my plan that is original, that is pleasant, that's all the things that I tried to be and tried to say musically. And it now has dawned on me -- and now that it has dawned on me, I am even more determined to try to improve that sound. And I still don't feel I'm as good as I would like to be. But it has been complimentary -- it has been these compliments that started me to playing music at the age of 12, and it has been that that has kept me playing music. It's the fact that someone like you and others has told me that I sound good.

Now, getting back to what we were talking about, in this conversation, if I were to explain why I sound good or anyone sounds good, I would have to say that it is the expression that comes from within you that makes you want to sound good or bad. You see?
Yes.

So subconsciously there was something that was happening in my life at an early age that made me want to sound good,musically, because it was something I wanted to say verbally that I couldn't say verbally that I could say musically. And it made me feel inspired to have many people come up and pat me on the back and say hey, that sounds good, and later on they started to paying me, which proved to me that it must be better than average.
Yes, that's right. That's right.
You know?
Yes.

But thank God for the humility that my father gave me, and my better knowledge and my ability to appraise my own talent as well as others. I know that I'm not as equipped as I should be and I didn't start out as equipped, but I think also this is a challenge that has kept me interested, more interested in music than the other things that I've done. And I'm proud to realize that it can make you happy, make you enjoy what I'm doing.
Yes, yes, you should be proud.
And I'd like to hear more from you about that.
All right.
Tell me more.

Well, what I want to know too is your approach to your talents. I mean, some people are burdened with their talents, there are people that are -- there are people that have to fight their talents. You know, I'm thinking of Ben Webster, for instance. Another -- I mean, he was tremendously talented and yet he had to fight that horn and fight himself and what not. And usually people that feel deeply too, you know.
But did you slave away at your talent or were you able to take it in your stride and develop it as you went along

Well, I think my approach to music is like most people, in fact you mentioned Ben Webster. And I happen to know quite a bit about Ben Webster as a person and as a human being and as a fellow who as I said my father gave me some instructions in psychology and what not at an early age. That makes it easy for me to detect certain peculiarities in people. And I think that Ben Webster probably had the same struggle that all musicians have, but it affected him differently and how he carried his self in personal life, and his habits and so forth, had to do with his atrocities --
Yes.

Or his confusion that you speak of. And I felt very close to Ben Webster. I believe he was born on the same astrological sign as I, Aries. And I admired his work, and the fact of the matter is if you want to speak in terms of competition, there was quite some controversy for the many early years of jazz that Ben Webster perhaps was classed as one of the top three or four tenor saxophone players in those days when there was Coleman Hawkins considered to be the father, the grandfather, and the originator of the true musical approach to the jazz saxophone, opposed to Lester Young's more loose expressions of down to earth playing and sounds of rhythmic meter.
And then there was Chu Berry who also had a different

musical approach. And Ben Webster had his own qualities, which was classified along with these great tenor saxophone players, you know. But as I said, I think that his struggle, and it's the same -- I think every artist in any field has this and I think they have to deal with this. And it comes apart in your life, and I've had my share of it and I'm having my share of it now. And you asked me did I struggle. Yes, I'm still struggling because it starts with your ability to improve yourself. And this comes in technical part of music like I'll never forget when I went to the army, one of the young guys caught me off guard, and he said you're a musician. I said, yes, I've been making a living playing music all my life. He said, how many sharps are there in F sharp, you know. You know, he caught me off guard. Right this minute I'm not too sure I can tell you.

I mean things of that sort are a challenge to you, no matter how great you are. And Ben Webster certainly was one of the most influential parts of Duke Ellington's band in the forties. Up to that point Duke's band had been featuring the saxophone more or less of Johnny Hodges. But Ben Webster actually gave Duke a new life, along with a bass player by the name of Jimmy Blanton. Between the two of these guys they brought new life to Duke Ellington's band, which made it able for him to compete musically with the other bands who were beginning to become popular, such as Count Basie and of
course Earl Hines who had always had a very fine rhythmic orchestration of musicians, you see.

So actually this struggle, I have had that struggle and I still have that struggle. This is part of being an artist, and particularly one who's making a living at the field. And in that sense I could say yes, I've had struggles and I'm still having struggles with myself, in trying to play.
And have had them from the start.

Absolutely. I've more than other people because I didn't really have the fundamental background, and I wasn't equipped musically, the knowledge. As I said, the time we're speaking of, when I started playing music, I had gone through three books of music. The John Williams book, I'll never forget it, and I became disgusted with it, the music, I became disgusted with the -- in fact it was this general conflict I'm telling you about this rebellion to discipline that made me rebellious against learning the proper fingering for scales. And which is very significant about jazz music because jazz music is what it is because of the origination of each stylist to play the way they feel and the way it's comfortable for them to feel.
According to their own equipment.
Right. Excuse me for cutting into your conversation, but to repeat what you said, according to their own equipment, see. And this is a great point in jazz music, and

without getting into the controversy of which is best or which is right, this is all part of jazz music, which at this time I would have to truthfully say -- I'd have to go out on a limb and say that it's a lot of controversy about what is good jazz and what is really jazz today.

Because in this period, they are mixing up all kinds of music. They play Latin music, they play what they call rock and roll music, which incidently going back to these early days the sound of rock and roll actually created a avenue,expression for the people who came up in what was known as black community as the holy rolly church. And they had ministers who were unorthodox, without license to preach, who had these large followings of black people, and they did all these dances which were sort of a primitive type, and chants because of this crazy dance. They used to dance, jump up in the air.

We youngsters used to go and see this, it was like going to a carnival to see these people do this, in our way of thinking. Because it was actually -- as far as the church laws, they were not really legal expressions of christianity. But it was an avenue to get to many uneducated people with christianity that wouldn't go to a church more disciplined. And out of this music came what today is known as rock and roll, you see.
Sanctified churches.

Yes. But to get back to my point, they have misconstrued the word jazz at this time by the inclusion of the liberal feeling and concept that all music is jazz or all music is good if it's played good. That's true, but after all you don't play football in a baseball park unless you play and get rid of the bases. You know.
Right.
You don't play basketball without the hoop.
There's form.
Yes, you see. Do you understand what I mean?
Yes.

So by that reason as I said there still is that struggle. I have it, everybody has it, you know. But the beautiful part about my beginning, and I would like to think my present participation in music, other fields as well as jazz, because I don't consider myself to be just a jazz player. The word means nothing to me except that high feel that the interpretation of the word jazz means not what the original Webster's dictionary said it was. I would like to quote from Webster's dictionary that I read some years ago when I was studying music, that Negro music was considered to be jazz, and they expressed it verbatim as to be loud and boisterous, negroid music. Was considered to be the term for

jazz. You see? So when we think of terms terminology we have to be very careful how we talk about things and how we interpret things because I've been fortunate to live through a couple periods, and that's why it's so difficult for young people to understand the disciplinary measures that were used by the old people and so forth and so on, because there's some things they don't understand, the why's, therefore's and all that you know, which has to do with it, you see.
Yes, yes.
But I said, it was my desire to express this happiness and the joy and beauty in me that made me decide to be a musician.

And perhaps it's the goodness of your background that came out in the expression of your feeling too perhaps, a background you may have been rebelling against in a way but which you respected and knew was good, whether it was good for you or not you did respect the goodness of it. And perhaps you know that sunny quality that comes out in your work, when you speak of happiness and joy and what not, perhaps some of that is derived from the background your father gave you. Could that be possible?
Well, I would like to think so. I mean, I don't normally like to get involved in theology, but in this type of interview, where what we're desiring to get

from me, you and I both, are the true facts of the way I feel, what's in me, what's going on within me. I would have to say that not only me but I think that everyone has a tendency to be brought back to the teachings that they had when they were children. If they've come up in a christian background I think they have to go back to the fundamentals of that christianity and their lives. Unless they are able to completely ignore them, like some people are, and I think that if they were brought up in another society I think that they would be brought back to their early teachings of that society.

But I've noticed in most fields of art, I think the nicer qualities are the most appreciated qualities by human beings, as we were discussing about human beings being flowers of the earth. I think that is very significant.
What was that you said exactly. When we were talking before you said that things that are created on earth, and you said that human beings are the flowers on the earth.
Yes.

But I went down with the rest of the people, and I remember getting some bacon or something like that, whatever they were giving away. But it wasn't in my family desirable for me to do that. But in other words -- but I took advantage of this situation, of the Civilian Conservation Corps enjoying the army, so that I could get away from the situation, get away from home.
You were about 17 were you?
I was exactly -- well I was 17 plus and by virtue of my turning 18 in a short time I was able to join. And also because of my ability to type. You know, there
was a need for clerical positions, and you know, people who could fill these clerical positions at the time.
You had learned that in school.

I had studied typing, yes. As I told you I studied everything that was given in the schools and I told you yesterday -- you asked me where had I learned my music, who was my supervisor. Well, in the public schools in America, which is one of the great things about America -- I want to get back to saying that because I think this is very important. Because even though I've been -- my father was a fighter for integration, and I have lived a life of integration all my life. Not by force, as I said, but by invitation.

And regardless of that, as I said, the United States of America, from my estimation from my travels, has got to be if not the greatest country in the world one of the greatest countries in the world, of all times. And I say that to say that to say this, that the music that I did learn, even though I was of a black race, and was underprivileged, I did have through the public schools an opportunity to learn music, through the public school system. And I always stress this when I'm talking to anybody about an interview, because I want that to be known and I want it to be understood that there is a way, and it has been shown in America that there is a way to work out racial conflict. And there has been improvements made.

It's unfortunate that some of it has come about by violence, but it is through the public schools that I learned how to play music, learned how to play the violin, went into the citywide orchestra because I was chosen by white supervisor who was teaching music and didn't show any bias. So I don't want to be recorded as one of those people who are so narrowminded as to feel that there is nothing right with America.
Yes.
Because I'm one of those people who thinks everything is right with America except no one is perfect, as America is not perfect. No country is perfect, no people are perfect.
Yes, right.
But I am very appreciative of this fact, that I did learn music in public schools. It was worth -- I may not have been able to afford the private lessons.
That's right.

Because I did have some private lessons, in fact there was one time in my life, during that period, that a lady offered to give me piano lessons in exchange to help her do housework in her spring cleaning. She was a teacher. And she had this big house, and I would help her do house cleaning, like you know, ordinary house cleaning.
Right.
And I guess she actually would have preferred to have a young boy like me who she wouldn't have to worry about a man molesting her or doing other things, or stealing something.
Yes.
She figured that I was more in line with someone she could take care of or wouldn't take advantage of her.
Right.
And then I did have the talent, and she was interested in me as a musician, and she gave me a few piano lessons in exchange for doing some housework for her.
That was very good, excellent, yes.
So in my life time, as I was speaking of my father, when I first started this conversation, I have been helped by numerous people of the caucasian race.
Yes.

I would say that it would even balance up to where I've had more help from white people than I've had from black, because I think that unfortunately during my childhood then it was only natural that the caucasian people were in a better position to help because they were more educated, as a whole.
And perhaps had a little more, were in a more fortunate position.
[We're in position to do it.]

Right. And I think this also has something to do with the style of music that I play. I'm sure it does because like I said, many of the artists who are entertainers, they learn to play from the background of the environment they were raised in, which was limited to an all black community or to circumstances which would not allow them to learn a different type of music. I was exposed to all kinds of music. So it has something to do with the way I play.
Yes, I'm sure it does. Well, I want to ask you, does that mean that you left to join the CC -- what was it called.
It was called the CC Camp.
CC Camp. Well, does that mean that you were robbed of your graduation of your high school?
That's exactly right. I had to leave school because of my choice, to get away from that environment, I really -- it was mainly that I thought that something might happen in the way of violence.
Yes. You were so appalled, really.
Yes, it just completely took me by shock.
Yes.
I had heard about it, I heard people talk about it, you know in fact many people, many black people

joke about it. In fact a lot of people wonder how do black people joke about these things that have passed, you know, and how they make it, you know. They look like they're having a good time all the time, which is not really necessarily true, like I told you about Fats Waller Fats Wallick.
Yes.
I don't think Fats Waller Fats Wallick was happy. Any human being who is intelligent enough to be able to produce art is ignorant enough to be happy with as the circumstances that is unpleasant.
That's right.
But they use alcohol or what not, or just gesture to overcome this to keep from being violent.
Right.
You see. The fact of the matter is I think people should be very, very appreciative and grateful that the masses of black people were really good people.
Yes, they were.

Because of the fact that they took whiskey and other things, parties, like the parties I played in. It was through the parties I played that people were able to give vent to their fears, and instead of fighting back, they just waited and bided their time until they could do something else --
Found what happiness they could.
That's right. And that's what -- that was possible
(Inaudible) to them.

Right. Which is a combination of what my music is about, what any true jazz is doing when they play music. And it's one of the reasons why I said, as we perhaps discuss before I finish why the jazz that's being played today that's categorized as jazz is not really real true jazz. You know?
I think it's a very interesting point.
Because they're not saying musically what jazz originally started out to say.
Yes.
Which is an expression, musically, of mainly this ability to offset madness with happiness.
Very good.
And there might be an interpretation of the real blues.
Very [Good] very well-done, yes. [PAUSE]

Well, that's a very interesting comment, and wouldn't you like to talk a little more about that, since your music is an expression of what is inside you and what's inside you is an expression of what you encounter in life?

Yes, of course. As I was saying about description of this blues, I think that it's very difficult to categorize music, it's very difficult to explain music, particularly to someone who doesn't know anything about

music. And I think even a discussion of notes, sharps, and flats have very little to do with music except that it's the way to play a note. You know, it's like a carpenter who learns how to drive a nail, but it doesn't necessarily tell him to where to put the nail, see.
Right.

And I'm sure that the original jazz and blues that was created by the great players of jazz music came about by the lives they had to live, which was similar to the situation I'm telling you about now that made me leave home. And by this same token, is the reason why someone who has not lived that particular life could never possibly give the expression of this type of music as someone who lived it. You see?
Yes.

So consequently there has been a change in the music you might say according to the change of times. And I think as the times have become confusing, in 1975, by virtue of all of the strife and struggles of that period, the music is in the same particular vein.
It reflects it.

It reflects the same thing, because there seems to be a constant struggle of people to find maybe their identity or to find peace of mind and in other words life goes on no matter what era. People have the blues and

people are unhappy and they are dissatisfied, and they haven't found any new way, I don't think, of really expressing these things. But in trying to express it in a new way, they have sort of distorted the true meaning in music.
Because actually there is a certain beauty in expression of the blues which has some sadness to it. But there I don't think is any way to express violence or bitterness unless you play bitter.
Yes.
Bitter sounds.
Yes.
You know?
Right.
Dissonant sounds.
Yes. Right.
Distortions.
Disturbed.
Loud. No shading of color. You know?
Yes, right.
Perhaps that might explain why there's so much difficulty in the younger musicians, or the musicians of this present era to express music with beauty as well as sadness.
Yes,yes, I think that's very true.
But without getting hooked up too far
into that I just thought I would mention that part because I think it's informative and interesting.
It is.
As I say about many things that I do say, --
It's very interesting. What I'd like to know factually too is what happened to your piano work when you went to CC Camp?

Well, that's where I think my career would begin as really a professional musician, ironically. I went in the army not knowing what I was going to do, or how I was going to do it. All I knew was that there was some sort of security in my mind, in joining the army. Not only was it an avenue of escape from that particular vicinity, you know, but it was also a sort of a feeling that -- well, I was being helped by being given some sort of employment, some way to occupy my mind and to use some of my talent, which would be appreciated and as well as I would be paid some money for it, and there was very little money. But there was some compensation. Part of the money was sent home to my family, which was to me a great gesture to pay my father back for all the money he spent on me.

And I got a little money on the side, and the funny part about it was once I got into this camp they picked out different people for certain jobs, according for what you were qualified for. And because I was small in stature, and

was a clerk typist, you know, by virtue of learning this trade, at school -- as I said, I was getting back to being taught these different things in school. I was also taught typing. And I was pretty good at it, and they needed a typist in the army, so I was the logical man for the job. So they chose me to be the company clerk.
Oh, I see.
Which not only that was a pretty good job, but I think it give me a little boost in pay. You know, perhaps of about six or eight dollars. You know what I mean?
Yes. In the army that's considerable, yes.
It made me close to the company commander whose name was [Mosey] Clark. I'll never forget his name, Captain [Mosey] Clark.
[Mosey.]
Of the 48th infantry. And he came from Kansas City. A very durable, great man.
Was he?
A caucasian man.
I see.

And I never will forget this. As I said it's significant, just as I had left Columbia, Missouri where a man, a black man had been lynched, the people in this area where we were sent, which was in the vicinity of Cape Jurado,
Missouri, near St. Louis, Missouri, in a little town called Delta, Missouri, company 3748, if you're interested in those facts --
Yes.

The people raised up and swore that they wasn't going to have these black guys in this neighborhood, no matter if they were members of the army. And this captain issued out the proper necessity ammunition and orders and said nobody's going to run the United States Army anywhere. We're going to stay here because we were sent here by the United States Government. And that was my first knowledge right immediately, that all white people were not people who hung black people. So you see that was very important.
Yes, yes.
Right away, immediately I was picked up in my spirits and I might have been a very violent man, you know, had this not happened to me.
Right.
But immediately, immediately upon leaving home and joining the army.
You saw that there could be justice.
I saw that there was justice.
Yes.
There was justice, you see.
Right.
And now --
Was it a black company?
It was predominantly black company, yes.
How many men in it, around?

I don't remember, there could have been 500. And we were dealing in conservation of land, you know, clearing wooded lands. I think now perhaps this is how the present freeways started, by the clearing of those swamp lands. And I -- at one time I got so disgusted I wanted to get out with the boys, I got mad at all that clerical work, and I should have been crazy, I must have been crazy because it was so easy it wasn't even funny. The rest of the guys had to go out in the mud and everything, and so I got mad and I jumped on the truck one day with my fatigues and my canteen, and they threw me off the lake like they'd thrown me in the lake that time at the golf course.
Yes.

As if to say get out of here buddy, go back in that office. Because -- well, not only that but they all loved me. This is really something that I would have to say, and I'm so happy, that the guys loved me. Because I played the piano in the mess hall, you know. In fact like I never had to worry about eating. You know how when the guys sit down to eat in the army, everybody sits down and you have to have what they call this boarding house reach. You
know, after they say the blessing and all, (noises). You know, I mean, and everything's gone.

If you don't have enough reach, it's like being an athlete or a basketball player, you really have to be like a basketball player. You have to reach way over there and get the bread, and get the butter and everything, and the milk is in the pitcher, you have to grab the pitcher. And you can just imagine -- and you can't spill it. You can't be a heathen. That's another thing about the army that's really great. It has discipline that is great for people, you know.
Now, imagine, all this is going on, and these guys are -- but nobody's spilling anything, because, you know, they don't allow it.
No, nothing's going to waste.
No, sir. But not only that, you're not allowed to be nasty.
Yes.

In the army. They won't tolerate it. You have to lie down and make your bed, just like they say in the boy scouts, you have to learn how to be a man, and be immaculate. In the army you have to make your bed every day. This is why the army is a good place for a lot of people who aren't able to go to school, or other things, because you can learn how to be a man. You can learn how to be somebody that
Yes.
You understand what I mean?
Because you have to learn, somewhere you have to be able to learn.

As they say nowadays, do you know where I'm coming from, man? Do you know what that means, do you know where I'm coming from? That's what they say. Do you know where I'm coming from, when I'm telling you about that self respect?
Yes, that's right, that's right.
You know?
Yes.
Which all gets back to my music, because this comes out in your music. And I'm convinced that all these things that I'm talking about have to do with the music, you know?
Yes.
And what may necessarily be the most popular music and the most profitable to the promoters and to the people who play it doesn't necessarily always have to be the best music.
No.
You know?
Oh, no, definitely.
And everybody can't be a Duke Ellington. You know.
No.
But I think that there's a lot of music to be expressed in this world, a lot of stories to be told and to be heard, musically.
Yes, yes.
As I'm telling you now they should be heard.
Yes.
There should be many, many stories.
Experience is translated into music.
That's right.
Yes. But you were saying that they loved you, and they loved you because you played piano and that made you popular with them.

That was one of the main reasons, yes. It had to be first, and naturally my talent to play piano made people feel good. Well, it was a combination of two things to me, because see, if someone's complimenting you, that makes you smile and feel good, so you automatically give to them.
That's right.

In other words that's-- I think that's one of the theories of christianity, although all these things are debatable. But there is much truth in it's better to give than receive. Because if you give in many instances, you will receive double.
Yes.
You see?
Yes.

You see what I mean, giving out my music that people complimented me, and they did things for me like all of the chefs. I never had to worry about grabbing this food, that's what I was trying to get around to telling you.
Yes.
I didn't have to worry about this, when they found out that I played the piano, because they would save my food for me.
Yes.
Because they liked to hear me play the piano.
Yes.
You see? And it was this compensation that went on and started my career. As I said, in the army as a company clerk.
Yes.
You see?
Yes.

And actually I went from zero on the thermometer to the top of the thermometer, with my inspirations. Because when I left home I was down to the bottom in spirit, I left with my head hanging down and just like a little alley dog, you know, with his tail curled under. Let me get out of town in a hurry. You know what I mean?
Yes.

And immediately my spirit was picked up completely, because I was surrounded by people who loved me and guys were happy and all men, and that's another thing, you see. There's something about men loving eachother that is different. I don't mean this --
I know.
-- freakish kind of love.
No.

I'm talking about manly love where another man loves you as a man, and grabs your hand, hey, man how are you feeling. Hey, how are you, baby, as they say now around, you know, hey baby, you know, hey, how's everything, you know, one of those things. You know what I mean?
Yes, I do.
You see, there's something about that that makes you great. So you see, (unintelligible) come on,
hey, baby, give me some skin. You know what they do, see, these are things that people don't know what they think that -- people are crazy.

See, after they're hitting the hands, like this together, hey, For instance you see (unintelligible) at the basketball games, at the football games. They come and introduce them, they hit eachother's hand like that, you know.
Yes.
That's love, that's togetherness.
Yes.
See? These are the things of course -- some people might consider this to be an illiterate way of expressing yourself, but it shows something.
No, I think it usually registers myself. I think it registers for what it is.
That's right.
I think people can see that well, I mean you see that there's lots of people that try to pick up on those habits out there. Huh?
I like the way you say pick up on those habits.
Right.
That pick up is a very, very famous saying too.
Yes.
It has many meanings about pick up.
Yes, it does. Well, this --
There's a song called 'Pick Yourself Up', incidently.
Is there? I didn't know that.
(Humming of song)
Oh, yes, that's right.
That's a very complicated song to play, would you believe it? It goes through three keys, it goes into four keys.
Does it?

The first part starts off, if you're going to play it for instance in the key -- here's something for you musical people who might know something about chord changes. Here's a little lesson for you from a jazz musician. I also sometimes have called chase, c-h-a-s-e. Do you know how I got that name? Because I used to sign my name C-h-a-s. which is the abbreviation for Charles.
Yes.

But we'll go into that later. I just wanted to give you a musical lesson, if you'll listen closely. This piece that I'm talking about, is it starts out in the key of -- you're going to play in the key of F.
Yes.
It starts out in the key of F for a little while, then it goes into the key of G for a little while,

then it goes into the key of A flat for a little while, in the middle, which is considered the middle part of the piece. And before it goes out of the middle part it goes into the key of C and then back to F.
And that's to be heard, is it?
That's right. Now, I don't want to go into details on --
Because you can hear that, the chord changes.
Right.
Is that right.
Now, I don't want to go into detail on that because that would take forever and a day.
That's very unusual, isn't it.

Yes. But anybody who knows anything about music knows something to think about. In fact the first time I played the number was much later in my career, and I didn't know the piece. Had a famous jazz musician who wanted to embarrass me, you know, a little friendly, you might say, gesture, in a way, you know.
Yes.
Well, I never could say truthfully whether it was friendly or not. You were-
(inaudible).
Like that --
Being tested.

He asked me if I knew the song and I said, no, I don't know that, but he knew I had a good ear, you know, so he challenged me, he said, oh, you know, he said you can hear it, you know. Now, this was in front of a lot of people you know.
Yes.
It was very embarrassing to me, and I played it so lousy it was a shame. But I never forgot it. Also it was a challenge to me.
But the other people also knew though, didn't they? They knew it was --
Well, there wasn't that many people playing. It was only a saxophone, a drums and bass and piano. So it was --
Yes, it was only the --
There was only two instruments playing lead notes, right.
Yeah, that's right, yes.
I won't call any names but this is also something interesting that goes on, people don't know, inside [jazz]
Yes.
Like you want to know what the coaches talk about you know (whispering), you know, when you
can't read his lips, you know.
Yes, right.
You know.
Well, listen, how long did that period of your life last, how long were you there then in that camp?

It seems to be the story of my life that I've never been any place too long. They say that Aries people are something like this, but I think that if i had a good way to express myself, and didn't have to worry about the economics of life, I think I'd stay someplace perhaps -- not forever but I think I'd probably stay there for a long time. Particularly at my age now. Let's see, how old am I? I think I'm a little bit older than Jack Benny was. I'm 40. Jack Benny stayed 39 for -- is that right?
That's right.
Well, I'm going to stay on 40.
You're just going to remain 40.
Yes, right. Just a little older than Jack Benny.
Yes, right.
On top of that such a lovely man.
Yes.
Very humorous. But I stayed in the army for 10 months to be exact, you know, and while I was in the army I would go into town on my leave. You know, every-

body would get a pass on certain occasions and I'd have to say because I was the company clerk, and getting back to why the guys liked me I'm also -- before I forget it, another reason why a lot of them like me is was because many of those guys were so uneducated that they couldn't write their names.
Yes.
And I had to sign an X for them on their payroll.
Yes.
So they'd get their money. So I became a savior to many of those guys, and the guy that got their money for them.
Yes, that's right.

But they all loved me and I loved them as men, and because I had this connection of helping them in that way, and I also played the piano in the mess hall. And then when I would go into town I'd play in these night clubs because at that time they had the famous jam sessions, j-a-m s-e-s-s-i-o-n which are now called jazz concerts.
Yes.

But the difference was that in those days they allowed you to do this, the musician's union allowed you to do this free, and different musicians who liked to play, and there were a few who could play, they would go around and get together with other musicians who wanted to play
and expressed themselves with ad lib music, because of their knowledge of the chord progressions, you see.
Yes.

In other words we would take pieces like Star Dust that was written by Hogie Carmichael, and very famous, and we would play the melody just long enough for you to know that we were playing 'Star Dust', and then we would start playing our ad lib versions and rhythmic conceptions of this piece. In our way these were known as jam sessions, like jam, you know, j-a-m.
Yes.
You see?
Yes.
Now they call them jazz concerts, right?
Yes.
Okay. And they get paid a lot of money for it.
Yes.
They get paid so much money for it it's not even funny, you know, the money that they get paid today I could have probably built a mansion with when I was coming up.
:Yes,yes, that's right.
You know what I mean?
Yes.

That's good, it shows that time moves on. But getting back to the story of that period, I would also be heard playing the piano in these different places, where people were having parties, and just like I played the house rent parties, many times in a night club they would always have a piano but no musicians.
Yes.
Because first of all there wouldn't be any musicians around in the town available. All of the best musicians would be in the larger cities playing with bands which were touring the country.
Yes.
You see?
Yes.

Not only that, but in the process I would sit in with these bands, some of them. Some of them may not have a good piano player, or a piano player who was capable of playing solo, or didn't have the personality, or maybe he got sick or something, or maybe he didn't get paid or he didn't show up because he didn't have any money to get to the job. And I would play in their place.
So I was constantly heard by the guys in the army, in CC Camp, and that brought about this warmness between myself and these men in the army.
Yes.
As well as other people.
Yes.
And I got to meet other people, you see?
Right.
And as I told you --
And you gained musical experience too, because you were playing with new people, if you sat in with other bands, and so on.
That's how I got started.
Yes.

Through that experience. Because the band came through there, as many bands did. They played this larger community. See our camp was located in Delta, Missouri, which was a little one horse town that the only thing I can remember about it is a wooden bridge that you cross over in a horse and buggy or something, you know.
Yes.
You know, like Mark Twain.
Yes.
Type of bridge, you know, that you read about in those stories.
Yes, that's right.
And then there was this other town called Cape Jurado, Missouri, which was a larger community and quite naturally it was in the larger communities that
the black orchestras were able to come out and play to a larger number of people and get paid for it, you see.
Draw.
Draw people.
Yes.

And so this Cape Jurado, Missouri had many of the name bands at that time, and then as I said it was common to hear all of the juke boxes which they were called at that time, juke boxes, the record players. Not they're stereos, hi-fi's. Same thing, record players, juke boxes that you put a nickel in, dime, three for a quarter, whatever. Only the famous musicians were heard on those juke boxes, you see, so if you had any kind of ear as a listener you knew the pieces, you recognized these artists. If you were a player of music you could recognize and learn these songs. And this is what we did, this is what I did.
I learned this music that I was listening to and hearing other musicians play, and I began to create my own image of these creations, you know.
Yes.

And as I said at this time there was Waller, Cab Calloway, Duke Ellington, Claude Hopkins. There's a difference between Claude Hopkins and Claude Thornhill, who comes later in my life. But they were all of these great musicians who looked up to and you admired

and you could learn from them. And they were mostly not only great and fine musicians, but believe it or not, even in those days most of these men were very intelligent type of people, clean cut people, well disciplined, well liked, dressed neat and had thousands of admirers. Because of their personal habits, which they didn't over exert themselves in these ways of, you know, deterioration of habits, you know.
Yes.
And those who might have some bad habits, people had a tendency to kind of keep them a secret.
Yes.

You know, people were ashamed to be seen, like even an alcoholic. Many musicians drink heavily, naturally because people are buying you drinks, and there were a lot of musicians who drank a lot of whiskey. In fact, by this time now, my age of 18, I was a professional drinker of alcohol.
Were you?
Of course, because it was right there. I mean, how are you going to refuse it.
Yes.
And it made you feel good. Alcohol makes you feel good. I don't care what nobody says, alcohol -- I've heard a lot of doctors say that alcohol is like medicine if you know how to handle it.
That's right.
If you keep the right thing in your stomach. You know?
Yes.
But it was all in fun.
Yes.

And of course the musicians who played music were fortunate enough to make a little money, have fun. And this is really what music was about, as far as jazz music was concerned, during that period. And it was, as I said, through meeting these musicians, coming through Cape (crossed out) Granby Jurado, Missouri, while in the CCC Camp, that I got an offer from one of these leaders to come to St. Louis, to play. Because he had had an argument with the piano player, his name was Cecil Scott, and he was a famous -- Tenor saxophone player. (Unintelligible).
(Unintelligible).
I don't -- all I remember about him is that he directed the band. This is another Cecil Scott, I think.
Oh, I see.
You see?
Yes.
And St. Louis, incidently, and Kansas City, were known jazz meccas. They were the known headquarters in the midwest for excellent jazz players. Many bands -- and
I remember another band I played with after I got there was DeShon Joe O. Shans, and they played all kinds of orchestrations. They were really professional musicians.
How do you spell DeShon?
D-e-s-h-o-n.
I see.
I think he was creole birth.
I see, from New Orleans.
From New Orleans.
Yes, yes.
Many of the creoles had a great influence on jazz music, the beginning of jazz, you see. And many of those creole people were great organizers, also.
Did you play in that band?
A short time.
Did you?
I didn't finish my story.
(Tape 4)

Well, Sir Charles, why don't you go on. You were telling us about your experiences in the CC Camp, and then how you would go into the town and play there, and come to know the visiting bands, and eventually you had an offer and you just had reached the point where you were going to join up, and why don't you tell us what happened after that?
Well, yes, I -- this band leader,

Cecil Scott, well, as I said, you know, when you go and play, guys like you're playing, and the musicians, you know, in a musician's world, you learn to play with someone else who can play or who can interpret your music, or can help you interpret. And a pianist in particular, especially in those times, more so than now, there weren't that many piano players who could play this music right. And the piano was more or less the leader of the group if you believe it or not because they depended on you playing the right chord progressions for them to hear what they were to play. Because of the musicians played strictly by ear.

Now, that doesn't mean that they couldn't read notes, because they read notes -- when you read an orchestration for the benefit of those who know music or even if you don't know music, when you play an orchestration, that's what you're doing. You're playing something that was written by someone else, and if you're playing in a large orchestra with more than one instrument, or several instruments, you're playing a part, like in a choral group like when you sing. You sing parts. There's a lead part and there's an alto part, a tenor part, the base part, so on, like a quartet. Same thing. You have parts.

Now, so you're reading the notes of the parts, the same as a piano player. The piano player is reading some notes and chord progressions, and like, you know, et cetera. But the thing about it is when you're playing ad lib you're

playing the chord progressions (which means) that you're leaving reading notes now and you're thinking in your head what chord is this I am to play in each one or two bars, a half a bar, or so many beats, and what not have you.

And so the piano player was like the leader because he had to play the right chord for them to hear what they were playing. And some of the musicians who didn't know these chords so well, they had the perfect pitch as I was speaking of, they could hear, believe it or not, what chord to play. You see?
Yes.

But the greatest musicians, the ones who were the leaders, like I mentioned before, like Coleman Hawkins and Roy Eldridge and many other great jazz players during that time, they were proficient inasmuch as they could read music, sight read music, and they could play chord progressions. And they were ahead of everybody else in that department. And most of the piano players who played, who were well versed, who had any kind of training at all, knew these chords. They didn't necessarily have to be good piano players but they knew the chords.
Yes.
In my case, I happened to be, which I will have to associate with my competitive feeling and spirit, as well as a desire to learn and a desire to want to be a part

of something, I was able to play the right chords and play solo. And having played solo piano by myself gave me the power and the strength and the knowledge to play with other people, and I was able to lead the other players as well as the boss players and the horn players, because my feeling was so strong and definite, in other words I knew what I was trying to do, and then I was always the type of person -- I never liked to do anything if I don't know what I'm doing. And I would try to learn the right chords to the piece. If I didn't I'd go and buy the music or learn it from someone who knew it.
Yes.

Which started me into my interests of writing music, because I wanted to learn, you see. But I still hadn't learned enough what I was learning, but I played well enough to be complimented by these musicians and to be wanted to replace this other piano player.
Could you play in any key?
I'll have to admit, no, I couldn't play in all keys so well.
At that time.
No. You know, there's -- in fact I think you could live all your life, and I don't think there's very many people who can play in all keys as well as they can play in others.
No.
This is one of the things we practiced, you know, playing in other keys. But at that time, you know, the jazz music was played in the key of C, F, B flat, E flat, and A flat.
Right.
But you sort of stayed away from those sharps.
Yes, right.
Because you couldn't get that many people to play in those keys, so you couldn't get to practice if you played in those keys.
That's right, yes.

You couldn't play with anybody because they couldn't play in those keys. Then there are some keys that are just not practical, just like life. You know, there's such a thing as making something too complicated, you know.
Yes. Quite right.
When it's too complicated it's no good.
No. And the key that might, you know, might possibly work out for you, is not going to be a good key for the alto or the tenor saxophone player, or even the (inaudible)
That's right.
And so on, because they're going to be in a different key too.
That's right. But as I said, as you get more proficient, and you get more experience, you learn to play in all keys, and be simple.
Yes.

But there are certain keys that lay in a position for the fingering of certain instruments that's better, also for the voice. For instance a tenor saxophone seems to be closer to the human voice of the average man's voice, you know.
Yes.
And the baritone has a rather base sound, you know. So all right, so there's a certain clef, a certain place --
A range.

A range, you see, for each instrument. Now, also the fingering. There are certain places that it's easier to finger, manipulate the fingers. Of course the pianist, he must have fingers, nimble fingers, and he must be able to do things that other people can't do, because he has to use both hands all over the key board. And you know, the other instruments like the saxophone, they have a special place to put their fingers, in a certain area, and then they change positions, they change registers. Then they can press down on a key which will change the register --
Control it.
-- and they just continue fingering in the same place.
That's right.
They don't have to move their hands.
No.
See, but a pianist must go up and down the piano, you know, and he has many more notes to read, which is very complicated.
It seems to me that nimbleness must have been something that you cultivated because compared to some piano players, your hands are small compared to an Earl Hines or --
I don't know, you haven't looked at them.
No, I wasn't looking (Inaudible). Are they not big?
No, my hands are very large.
Are they?
Look there.
Now what is your reach then?
Well, I can reach way over a tenth.
You can?
Yes, I can reach actually --
I am surprised.
Not practical, because a tenth is just about the most practical thing that you can reach.
Yes.
And I can reach a tenth very easily, which in fact is very comfortable for me to reach a tenth.
Were your hands always well developed or did that -- or did you develop them? To play.
Well, naturally they were developed more from playing music.
Yes.
Naturally, practicing on the scales.
That was very fortunate, wasn't it.
Oh, yes, of course. But I think most all musicians have well coordinated hands on any instrument.
Yes.
Your hands become stronger and more agile.
Yes.
Because they have to be.
Yes.
It's coordination of your --
Continual use of them, yes.
Right. It's a coordination of your mind and your fingers, and they must be simultaneous.
Right.
But I don't think mine are faster than
anybody else's, however, as I said, it's just -- it's part of your training, you know.
Yes.
Of course as I said, I think feeling and depth of conception have a lot to do with this also. You see, as I said, being athletic inclined I think is an asset to a musician. Having the rhythm.
Yes.
Because, you see, in order to be a good athlete you must have good rhythm.
Yes.
And music -- you take a lot of your great athletes. They like music. They might not know music but they have a sense -- very sensitive to the beat, rhythm, you know.
Yes, right.
And this is what is a pulsation of the popularity of music, is the sense of rhythm.
Yes.

Not so much the melody necessarily, although some music reaches people more from the melody than the rhythm, you see. And then it's controversial really, because, I mean, there are so many people who like melodies who don't even know anything about rhythm. They can't even pat to the beat.
That's right.
But this is going into very technical musical terms which --
Yes,we ought to keep this for a little later on, in the development of your career.
Yes. Getting back to this --
Go back to --
Atmosphere.
Yes. In fact (unintelligible) to Cecil Scott perhaps.

Yes, right, right. Well, before -- in fact, before I go into that, though, I would like to say that I made an error in saying where my music started. I forgot about one particular case that I told you about just now?
Yes.
Before we came back to the tape, that I'd forgotten about. Before I had went into the army -- I must have been -- now at that time, I said 12, I said give or take, right?
Yes.

So I must have been around 14 when this first surge into the music business hit me. We were in a town -- my father was preaching at a town, a church in a town Carthage, Missouri, C-a-r-t-h-a-g-e, Missouri. And we lived there and as I said my desire to pick up a little extra cash for myself, now was beginning to want more clothes, and I was called

embarrassed to ask my father for extra money because he might buy me a suit, you know, two pair of pants. But I'd want an extra pair of pants, or some shoes to go with it. So in order to buy the things that I wanted I needed to get some extra money.

So I went out and got a job as a shoe shine boy, and I wanted to show you a little something that used to make me a little money when I was shining shoes. If I can get the sound here (humming). See, I would take my rag and shine shoes like that. After having cleaned the horse manure off some of the shoes of some of the cowboys that'd come in, and they would only give you a dime, you know. But sometimes some of the more high class people would throw a little tip in there if I'd take the rag and pop it like that (humming). And they guy would say, that's a good shine, (can) you do that again. (Humming). Yeah, man, give me 15 cents.
So I'd get 15 cents for the shine, you know, maybe a quarter, you know.
Right, yes.

And in fact, I had such a personality really, and I'll tell you as I live here, alive today, I did not really do this out of ego, I didn't do this out of anything to show off, it's just something that happened natural-ly. I wanted some money, you know, and the people -- some of these people, you know, like they just would -- this would be
a reason for them to give me extra money, to have me do this, and it was like show business.
Yes.

Now, right down the street, adjacent to the hotel, the barbershop was part of the hotel, I was working in a barber shop -- I don't know whether I mentioned this or not at first. But I was the porter and the shoe shine boy in the barber shop, which had about four seats, four chairs, which catered to all the people in the hotel, and the downtown business people like the dentists, the lawyers, and the what do you call the main building, the city hall?
Yes.

That's what you find in most all the cities, and all these small towns, they have a little circle there. They call that the downtown area, you know. Well, now the theatre where they had all the shows come in, the travelling shows came in was right next door to the hotel, and they all stayed in there, right. So this gave me this inspiration, and I played the ukelele, you know, four string ukelele, and I'd sing. You know, this was all during the time of Bing Crosby, the Mills Brothers, you know, right?
Yes.
(Singing). One of those things, Mills Brothers (Humming). You know, right?
Right.
So this is all inspiring me and I'm a young boy, you know, I'm having fun, and getting paid for it, getting paid for it, you know, getting paid, spelled g-i-t-t-i-n', gittin' paid.
Right, gittin' paid.
Gittin' paid, baby. You know, right on.
How long did you do that?
Oh, as I told you, my amnesia was already starting then. I don't know how long it was. It seemed like just a short time. Everything --
As long as your father was --
As long as we were in that town.
Yes, right.

But wait a minute. Further, to make money, to show you how my life was always -- I was always trying to do something for myself, you know, to be independent. I also became very good at washing and polishing cars, which I got an extra fee for this, naturally. And I'd take the cars in the back and wash them up and shine them up, and some of the very nice guys would let me take the car for dinner and I'd go and show off in front of the girls in school. You know, they'd think I had a new car every day. You know, this made me a little popular with the girls, too, you know.
Of course.
So I was beginning to like girls, you know.
Sure.
As every boy does, you know.
That's right.

He can't get rid of that feeling, you know, so easily, you know. Right? So all this was a part of my having fun, and actually as I said this is before I had noticed this vicious thing. I was happy and enjoying myself, and my music was what did it because my music put me in such a realm above everything that I didn't even hardly see these ugly things.
No.
Because I was so busy having fun, and it didn't strike me individually, see.
That's right.

So I was having fun as a young boy. So in the process all of the entertainers that came there, I was also bellboy. Now, how do you like that, at 14 years old? I was a shoe shine boy, I was the porter, and I helped bells at night. Right?
Right.
All of which I got about $2.50 a day, maybe a week. I don't know. But I got tips, you know, and I played my little ukelele. So all the entertainers, they knew
me, and you know, I got these little tips, and you know, made a little name for myself in the town there.
Yes.

As an entertainer. And I'd play my ukulele, sing one of my songs, you know. (Singing). You know, what I mean, pop my little rag. Right? So that's really how I got introduced to the entertainment business period, I mean, you know, gradually I was getting into it then, before I told you I went to Columbia, Missouri, to high school.
Right.
See, I was in grade school during this time.
Yes.
But don't you think that's very interesting?
Yes, I do.
I don't know how I forgot that.
So I mean you had a real first taste of the entertainment world, didn't you? Yes.
That's right.
Well, now, tell me, I'm very eager to hear about the first band and how it happened, how it worked.
Well, that was a flop.
Was it?
I might say. Yes. It was my first

attempt and it was completely flopped. But however it was also a great lesson for me not only in music but in life, because I wasn't prepared, and I found out that I wasn't prepared very soon. Now, the band leader was mad at the piano player. he had working for him, who was very, very good. He was a good piano player, he was educated, and he played good music, and he wrote arrangements. Which could be the reason why I was challenged to learn all these things later.
And I went to St. Louis and to join this band. But when I got there I couldn't read music fast enough because I hadn't had the training.
You hadn't had the experience.

I hadn't had the training and the experience. And at that time you had to read the notes, you know, they had the notes and there was a lot of notes to read. And I hadn't had experience. A young guy. In other words I wasn't good enough, let's put it that way. Just frankly.
Yes.
Well, now I didn't know this, and the band leader didn't know it, because he didn't try me out ahead of time. And all he knew was I could play, that I could play.
Yes.
You know, ad lib solos. Which was important. But that wasn't the most important thing, see. And

so I sort of jumped the gun and I gave up my position as a clerk typist in the army, which I got an administrative discharge to accept better employment. That was the legal reading of my papers, of my discharge, in other words, you know; in other words there were several types of discharges. The honorable discharge was the ordinary discharge of the army for ordinary purposes, you know, and then of course there were dishonorable discharges for unpleasant things, in fact I remember making out several dishonorable discharges which had to do with the behavior of some of the men in the army, which wasn't desirable.
Yes.

You know? But mine was known as an administrative discharge, because I was leaving my position to accept other employment. And so I left the CC camp and went to St. Louis, and that's where I first got my blues, my taste of the blues. (Singing).
Yes, your first blues are very blue, aren't they?
Yes, don't you know it. It's like a woman's first love going sour, you know?
Yes.
You think a man loves you like you love him, you find out he don't care that much at all. My goodness gracious, I've got the blues, I've got the blues so bad.
So what --
Because I've been had.
What happened to you, were you stranded or what happened?

Absolutely. Absolutely. I was stranded in every sense of the word. I went to St. Louis and I couldn't cut it, I couldn't play the music and I was so embarrassed, and naturally -- but I mean, what could you do. The guy couldn't use me. He recommended me to another band leader who was using a girl pianist because he didn't have a man who could play, and he would prefer to have a man but I couldn't read the music, I couldn't read that music good enough. I didn't have experience. And so there was nothing for me to do. They couldn't use me, you know. Unfortunate, it was just unfortunate, you know.
You were frightened.

No, I wasn't frightened, no, because believe it or not I had made friends there, and I never will forget the family I stayed with. I stayed at their house like a relative. People were like that during those days, particularly if you were a musician or entertainer, you know, because they'd realize that you had this talent and they tried to help you because that was in their appreciation for your talent.
You haven't told me what year it was.
Wait a minute now, let's see. You
Well, no, let's just think. You were 17?
Well, I was 18. I would have to be 18.
And you were born in 1918.
I was born in 1918.
So it was 1936?
Is that right?
I think so.
Let's figure this out.
No, that's all right, it's 1936, it's two 18's.
It is?
Yes.
I believe you're right.
I think so.
I believe you're right.
And we don't have to swear on the bible or anything but it's 1936.
Now, that shows you how much smarter you are than I am.
But that's what it is because that's interesting to know just what period that was.
Yes, well I'm glad you brought it up because like I said I'm very lax in facts like that.
Yes.
And I must --

Well, you see, people listening to you will want to relate it to what's happening in other places at that time, in those years. You know. So 1936. Well, then so what did you do? You stayed with these people, and what did you do?

I stayed with this family for a short time, I don't know how many -- perhaps a couple of weeks or maybe, you know, for awhile, while I explored the city of St. Louis, which incidently I got a chance to meet the great jazz musicians who were there then, and there were a lot of musicians coming in and out of there, from that town.
Who for instance?
Well, this band -- I can't name all of them now but I -- by name at this moment, but all the great bands that played in the midwest, they either came from St. Louis or Kansas City.
Well, just like Jay McShann.
No, Jay McShann was from Kansas City.
Yes.
And he was also from a later time than this, because Jay McShann is about my age.
Yes.
He was coming up in Kansas City, which
I went to school there later, which I'm going to get to --
And you don't mean Benny Moten, because that was before that.

Benny Moten came from around Kansas City. See, the St. Louis bands were t--they -- I -- you might consider them sort of like a band -- let's see, oh, I can't remember their names now. It's just not clear to me. I can go into the history and speak of it, but if you associate the year that I'm talking about with the band that you find in the history books, you would realize who I'm talking about. Fate Marabel was one of them.
Marable
Yes, yes, I see.

And those bands. Because -- in other words St. Louis -- the two midwestern cities were divided, and St. Louis actually had a different brand of musician than Kansas City. St. Louis had a more organized, polished orchestra type. They played a lot of stock arrangements and that sort of thing, and they had some pretty good singers.
More polished.
Well, no, I wouldn't say more polished, just a different type of music.
I see.
Kansas City had the real hip music, because as you know, Kansas City was quite a town for night life, see.
Yes.
You understand what I mean?
Right.

And St. Louis was more of a town of a little more maybe educational facilities. Incidentally, when I went to Kansas City later I got to know most of the great jazz musicians who I became associated with later in some way, including Count Basie, and Lester Young.
Yes.

But getting back to the St. Louis story, as I said most entertainers, musicians, in the old days, in the black community, if they had any personality at all, the people learned to like you. Not just because you were a musician but as I said you learned how to live with people, and you realize that it was quite a compliment to have people like you and help you, and you needed assistance, and it wasn't uncommon that people would often take you in their homes as a part of the family, you know.
Yes.

And you know, if you didn't have any money they realized that you didn't work regularly and they would wait until you got the money to pay for the rent or you'd sort of go -- you know, what they call -- what do they call it, Dutch lunch.
Yes.
You know, when you go Dutch.
Going Dutch, yes.

You put in, and everybody chip in and buy some food or something like that. And it was not uncommon that people would be that kind to you, which is all the more reason why I said I'm more appreciative of the public as a general, particularly people who like my music. Because all of my life it has been the people who have liked my music who have made it possible for me to continue on to play music. Because the type of music that I play, and that I like to play, which is known as jazz or created music from the soul of your imagination, which is done more or less spasmodically and simultaneously at the time that you're on the job or playing an engagement, you know, it's not the type of music that is considered commercial.
No.
You know. People don't normally pay people to play that kind of music, you see.
Yes. It isn't everybody that appreciates it that hears it.
Right. Like I told you about the girl that thought it was noise.
Yes.
Like the difference being so that

anyone else could understand is like Lawrence Welk for instance, who has a wonderful organization that he plays all kinds of popular melodies, and people can understand his music who like melodies and who like to dance just ordinary dancing or socializing. And remember the old songs.

You see, there's a difference in the music he plays and jazz music inasmuch as it is all music, but it has a different expression. And it's almost like a language. It is. I'm convinced that jazz music is like a language, and you have to speak that language to understand it. And so consequently the people who speak that language, or like anybody else who speaks a foreign language and finds somebody who understands their language like for instance they're happy to see them. Oh, hey, you know. And it's the same way with jazz people.

But these people were very friendly to me, but however by the same token we all have an amount of pride. You know, we don't want to live on charity, and so after a short period of time when I realized that I wasn't good enough to make a living at the thing that I was doing, I realized that my lack of experience, my age, and lack of ability to earn money, made it necessary for me to go back home. And here again my father came to my aid, as he always did, and to protect my interests he sent me a ticket in care of the Traveller's Aid Society.
I've had an occasion in my life to appreciate all the services of many fine organizations which you've heard me

name from time to time. That was one of them, the Traveller's Aid Society. In other words that was what those people did, they helped people who were in trouble or something like that, like today you find that a lot of these people who help wayward girls or girls who are pregnant without a father, without a husband, that was the type of thing that was -- and my father being rather crafty, knowing that if he sent me the money I might spend it.
Yes.

He was sure if he sent that ticket in care of the Traveller's Aid it couldn't be cashed, and I had to come home. Which I did. And that's when I went back home and that's when we came into the period when I really started to study and tried to learn how to become a jazz musician because I'd had enough experience and enough taste of it to know that I really wanted to do that. I had an inclination to be a musician, and whatever you want to call it. Now, they call it jazz. I just wanted to play music. And the other people called it jazz, but I wanted to play music, I wanted to express myself, you see.
Yes.
So now in the meanwhile my father had moved from Columbia, Missouri, where I had to gone in the CC Camp to Parsons, Kansas, you see.
Yes.
He had moved in these 10 months he had moved to another city.
Right.
See?
Yeah.
And that's where I really got introduced to jazz formally by Wilbur, W-i-l-b-u-r, known as Buck, B-u-c-k, last name Clayton, C-l-a-y-t-o-n.
Now, Sir Charles, what did Buck mean to you, where did you meet him, and what came off that meeting?

I met Buck Clayton in Parsons, Kansas at a house right down the street from where we lived. And there was a girl there who had a piano and she was not a good pianist but she was interested in music, and several of the guys in the neighborhood, including myself, were interested in her. And in that town Buck Clayton had come home to visit his parents. His father was a minister in that town, and there was another famous musician whose name was Bill Davis, the organist. His father was a minister there, and we were all in this town at the same time, and so we had a jam session at this girls' house, and Buck played. He had just come back from China not too long before that and he had joined Count Basie's band which was playing Kansas City at this time.

Now, what I forgot to tell you was during a period of my school days I had been going to school in Kansas City,

Kansas, which was just across the river from Kansas City, Missouri. And I had met Charlie Parker at that time who became famous later. And I had heard a lot of these jazz musicians and I got this sound in my ear, you know. I didn't go in the night clubs but I had heard these musicians at jam sessions. And that's when Charlie Parker started out.

And so I had had this association in Kansas City, Kansas with the Kansas City music, which was the real music of the night life crowd, which later on became so famous with Count Basie. So Buck Clayton was working with Count Basie, and I was so impressed with his playing and his looks. He was a very, very clean, intelligent man who convinced me that jazz musicians were also gentlemen and intelligent people, not necessarily the drunks that people had thought that they were -- all were.
And so in other words I didn't think that I'd be going too far away from my keeping to play music, because Buck Clayton happened to be the son of a minister too and was doing very well.
Right.

And I had played a lot of parties around there and dances, as I said, solo piano playing at parties. So it was then that I knew that I wanted to be a musician. And a band came through there, a very, very raggedy type of band. You know, they weren't too good. You called them tramp

bands in those days. His name was Warren Webb. And he needed a piano player, so they waited for me until the next day, because I couldn't convince my father that I should go out again. But he let me be my own man, and he tried to discourage me. He wanted me to go to college, but he knew that I was going so he finally just -- I went off with this band.
And we went to Omaha, Nebraska, where I joined this band called Warren Webb, and these are some of the questions that I think that you're interested in.

Yes, I am. Yes, I am. Well, in staying with that band you began to be able to cope with reading the music, for instance, or your reading was improving that much, was it? Or had it already improved that much?

Yes. I had been challenged and I had been encouraged to study more. Now, this all comes slowly and it came slowly. And I'm still studying music as most musicians do. So in my desire to better myself I realized that I had to study, so in the process I started to studying music more seriously, and learning to read better, and also learning to write. And it was during this time that I left this first band that I played with, because they weren't working regularly enough and I had learned from the experience in St. Louis that I had to make money as well as enjoy, so I joined a more successful band known as Lloyd Hunter.
Yes, I see. How long did you stay with Lloyd Hunter?
I stayed with Lloyd Hunter for several months and then I joined another band which was a better band, by the name of Nat Towles.
Yes.
