And it was in these bands, after I had played for a short time in a night club in Omaha, Nebraska called Jim Bells that I had learned to write music rather well, and I was considered to be one of the good jazz arrangers in that area.
That was very quickly done from over a period of what, about 18 months. All that.
Right, right, right. In that period I learned to write music.
Did you -- were you self taught, learning to write music?

More or less, more or less. As I said my knowledge of studying music in school, I had the fundamental basics, and I learned from other musicians. I had little sessions, you know, we got together, people were friendly, and musicians exchanged ideas. And I studied arranging on my own. I got the books and I read them, and you know, you go to the library and you pick up a few books here and there, and you talk to a few experts. And I also had the feeling of
jazz, which was important in writing this music, you see.
So that your arrangements carried that flavor. Well, now Nat Towles' band, Buddy Tate was in that band, wasn't he?
Yes, Buddy Tate was the main featured soloist in that band.
Yes.

He was a very good solo player, and Buddy had had much experience, and he was a very, very nice person, and a lot of personality. And the fact of the matter is Buddy Tate was very instrumental in helping me learn a lot of the things that I learned about music, and of course we had a very warm friendship because he liked to play and practice, and I was always willing to practice and play with him. And we learned a lot from eachother.
That's wonderful.
Yes.
Who else was in the band, Nat Towles' band. There were a number of musicians who made a success in New York afterwards, weren't there?
Well, there was some. Henry Coker later on --
Yes, went with Basie.
-- became a member of Count Basie's orchestra. He was a very, very wonderful trumpet -- trombone
player, still is. And in fact he was one of the most excellent trombone players I've ever heard in my life, and still is -- I consider him to be one of the greatest trombone players in the world.
And there was also a saxophonist by the name of Charles Price, known as C. Q. Price.
Oh, yes.
He was quite an arranger, and saxophonist. He later went with Count Basie, after having played a little while with Horace Henderson's band.
Right.
And there was another very good friend of mine named Bob Dorsey who was also in that band. He took Buddy Tate's place when Buddy Tate joined Count Basie.
Right.

It was during that time, in the late thirties, '38 or '39, somewhere around there, that Count Basie had a misfortune with one of his famous saxophonists. Herschel Evans died, and he called Buddy Tate to take his place.
Yes.
So we had to have someone to take Buddy's place, and it was this friend of mine, Robert Dorsey, who was a very excellent saxophonist.
And who did he go to afterwards?
He joined Horace Henderson's band along

with some of the other musicians around Omaha; the drummer's name was Debo Mills who I played with with Lloyd Hunter who was a great jazz drummer. and he was with some other musicians. I can't remember all of their names.
How do you spell Debo?
D-e-b-o. Isn't that odd? Debo Mills. M-i-i-l-l-s.
Oh, yes, right.
He was a great drummer, a great drummer, great drummer.
Well, how long did you stay with Nat Towles. And I see you went to Floyd Roy's band from Nat Towles. How did that happen?
Here again I'm lost for statistics. I don't know time, I just can't -- you see --
To think back that far you can't remember how long.
I'm not good at statistics. I would have to really go back and get records and so forth, which I don't have personally.
No.

But I'd also like to mention while we're talking about that, that this first band that I played in had a very, very important figure in the world of entertainment in the midwest, in the person of Anna Mae Windburn.
Oh?
She was a girl singer who directed Lloyd Hunter's band.
Oh. (Inaudible).

Yes. She was very good at this too. She handled the baton to the beat of jazz music, and she sang. Very, very pretty girl, very attractive girl. And she led the band while we played, she was part of the attraction.
Did they ever made any records?
I don't think so.
No.
She later on went on to lead the girls' band. You know, they had several --
Not the Sweethearts of Rhythm?
The Sweethearts of Rhythm, yes.
Really?
That's right. That was Anna Mae Windburn, and she was the girl vocalist in the band that I first played with. Lloyd Hunter was the first good professional band that I played with.
Is that right?

And she was the singer and band leader in that group. We also had another singer by the name of Red Rivers who did a lot of tunes of entertainment, like one of his famous songs was Old Man Moses Kicked the Bucket.
Yes.
You know?
Yes, yes, I remember.
Old Man Moses. Old Man Moses. Old Man Moses, Old Man Moses (Singing).
I remember that That Stuff made a hit with it too.
Right.
Do you remember [____].
Well, this fella was very proficient at doing these entertainment type of numbers, and the two of them led the band.
Yes.

He would lead the band when he was singing his numbers, and they had quite a trick and art of using batons of doing this with, see. But you asked me how long I was with Nat Towles. I was with Nat Towles for several -- oh, I'd say at least a year, perhaps. We travelled mainly through the midwest in the summer months, and we would go south in the winter months. We played regularly, annually at the Mardi Gras in New Orleans, and we used to play what they call battle of music with another band called -- let's see, I can't think of his name. There was another -- a creole band in New Orleans that was quite good. And we used to play with them every year, and they had this celebration down there.
And jazz was very popular in the south, you know.
Yes.

And people were happy. They really had good times and they -- as I said, the economic situation had no bearing on the feelings, and that's why I say jazz really acted as an anecdote to me, and as a medicine. And I think it also was medicine to people of that time.
Yes, I'm sure it was. Yes.
You know, it helped people to forget.
I'm sure it was. Well, you went to Floyd Ray's band from -- you moved to California with Floyd Ray's band. Well, what was Floyd Ray's band like?

Floyd Ray had an excellent band, musical band, and entertaining. He had three singers with him, three girl singers. Three girl singers, and they had made a famous record called 'Three O'Clock in the Morning.' A beautiful arrangement. He had several very good arrangers from the west coast who were writing for the band, and he had great musicians in the band. Good, very good organized group.
Can you remember any?
I don't remember all of their names.
Any that perhaps ended up on the east coast?
No, none of the musicians in this band really turned out to be great jazz players. They were more or
less --
Section men.

Section men, and they worked well together. They had a lot of good arrangements. That was about the size of that band. The fact of the matter is it really wasn't built around solo players like the great jazz groups in the world, but however my reason for joining the band was that after Buddy Tate left Nat Towles', several other things happened that sort of took the interest out of the band, you know, because jazz music is music that is played inspiringly, and sometimes the musicians in the group make the band sound good and inspire the other players.
Yes.

Some of them who may not be as well equipped to play solo, they like to back up the good players, you see. So part of the inspiration and fun had sort of diminished in Nat Towles' band, and at that time then I was trying always to move on to better things, and I met Lester Young, the great tenor saxophone player, and Joe Jones, in Omaha, Nebraska, while I was playing with Nat Towles. Because Count Basie at this time now had became famous, and his music was becoming famous, and the players in his band became famous, and all of the jazz players as I told you, particularly people like Louis Armstrong, and these kind of people, were always happy to lucky people, willing to encourage younger

musicians at any chance that they got. And so by meeting Lester Young and Joe Jones, I was inspired, and as I was inspired naturally you wanted to go onto better things. And none of these orchestras that I played with had a full amount of men who were qualified to be good players.

We had perhaps like one or two good solo men like Buddy Tate, and maybe a trumpet player or trombone player. Like Henry Coker played trombone. And there was another fella by the name of Henry Beckett who played beautiful trombone. He had a sound like Tommy Dorsey and he played with a feeling of the blues, you know. And we had several good players, but it was limited.
Yes.
We had say like 12 or 14 men, and out of 12 or 14 men there would be about a half a dozen that might be able to play a decent solo, maybe two were very good.
Yes.
So you can see, I was always striving to associate with better musicians, and improve myself, because that's the way I was learning by surrounding myself with better musicians.
But Lester in those days -- Lester wasn't exactly as approachable musician as some other musicians, was he? I mean, wasn't -- Lester was a loner in a way, was he not?
Yes, but you see, that's the strange

part about it. Lester was a loner to people who didn't know him, and he only -- he kept himself restricted to only the people he wanted to know. He only got warm with people he wanted to know, because most of the people didn't understand the music, and didn't appreciate him and showed signs of it, so he rebelled against it.

But a musician who could play fairly well, or was good enough to make an impression on him, or that he liked to play with, and that he heard something he liked, he was very warm. He was not the same cold person that he seemed to be to other people.
Right.

And that's the way -- it's like a clique, click if you want to call it, whatever. But it's like sports or anything else, if you can do something well, you know, or if you can do something that someone else appreciates, and they do the same thing, you have a natural tendency.
Yes.

It's just like you and I talking here. You have an appreciation as an interviewer of what I'm doing and what others are doing that makes you interested. Whereas someone else who didn't have an appreciation for it wouldn't care if they talked to me ever about it.
Right, right.
Or wouldn't care if I existed.
Right.
You see.

Of course Joe Jones was a different sort of a person, a very -- an extrovert, Joe, a marvelous drummer. Was Joe a person that you related to let's say not exactly intellectually but -- well, I can better understand you and Lester be close than you and Joe.

Yes, well there again as I said, all of these people with talent, for some reason or other, always seeked out younger musicians or other musicians who had signs of either had talent or showed signs of talent. I'd have to say in this case I was a young fella who showed signs of promising some talent. I had -- I must have had some talent to show that I had promise of other talent. They were further advanced than I was, but my keen interest -- and as I said, which is important, I was always seeking to learn. And so naturally I admired these musicians and I put myself in the position whereas they respected my inquiry, and I was respectful of them, and I think that they learned to respect me and like me because I was interested.
That's right.
And they felt that they could show me something.
Instinctively helped.
Right. And so in other words as I said,

where these people would be hard to understand by others, who didn't fit in the environment or in this circle of musicians, well, I had no problems because they loved me. Well, now in the sense of the word. For instance I would have to say that Lester Young loved me because I later on played with them and he expressed his love for me warmly. Now, in the case of Jo Jones being another type of person, Jo Jones always was considered -- I think he considers himself and he acts in the form of a teacher. He always wanted to teach people, young guys. If he felt like he had an obligation. That's his personality.
Yes.
And he enjoyed playing.
Yes.

And he still does. In other words, he enjoyed playing, and like, you know, when he played in a band, you're restricted to the four or five hours that you're playing a job, so -- and then you're restricted to a few solos. Now jazz music is based on solo work, ad lib, see. So -- all right, so you're just getting warmed up. So that's what caused this -- that's what brought about the jam sessions that I told you about before, because musicians want to play. And they don't get a chance to play enough in a big band where they've got 14 pieces, and guys singing and playing a little bit of this, and you've got to play music to people that want

to play it that you don't want to play, and you've got to play a part. We had just warmed up to play your instrument. Because you want to play, you want to experiment, you want to hear yourself playing, you want to get this feeling you will enjoy. And you're wide awake, you know, you're just ready to go when the dance is over, see.
Yes, right.
And this is what Lester Young and the older musicians did. They'd go around and play with whoever -- whatever musicians they found in the town could play.
And this is really where you knew them that way.
That's right, I met --
Because you were there doing the same thing.
Right, I met Joe Jones in this place that I told you I played before I went with these bands. I was playing a place called Jim Bells' night club. I was hired there by the owner.
This is Omaha?
Omaha, Nebraska.
Yes, right.
You see, the club owner hired me through a relative of Joe Jones, incidentally, who was a singer named Wynonie Harris.
Oh, I know.
You've heard of him.
Yes.
The blues singer, right?
Yes, yes.

So you see all of these people tie in together. It's like a convention, it's like an organization. You know, word gets around that there's a young guy that can play, you know, like Duke Ellington. That's how he hired Jimmy Blanton. He had several choices of musicians to hire from. He heard about a bass player in Minnesota by the name of Oscar Pettiford that was very good, and he heard another one in St. Louis by the name of Jim Blanton, so he chose Jimmy Blanton because the word got around that he had talent. More so than today.
Because when you had a little talent in those days it stood out like a -- not a sore thumb but like a green thumb.
That's right. Very good.
And that's how I met Lester Young and George Jones.

Yes. Well, look then when you got to the coast with Lloyd Hunter -- no you got to the coast with Floyd Ray rather, and you did studio sessions. Did you stay with Floyd Ray's band, do you remember that.
No, I didn't.
You came to California and you moved into studio work?

No, no, that's not true. I didn't play studio work. There again as I said, I was still learning, I was still -- I considered myself to be actually still in my embryo stage of learning. I was slowly learning. I had learned how to write music, but I still was not sure that I was a competent writer. I knew I was writing to write notes, but I didn't have the real professional feeling where I would say I was in demand by the famous orchestras. I hadn't learned that yet.
No.

I was still learning, still studying. I kept my head in the books, I kept my head in the library of music, I kept listening to music. And not only that, but this is where at the time when I got to California that I met Art Tatum.
Oh.
The lord and god of not only the piano but music.
Really?
That's right. To me Art Tatum says everything there is to be said about jazz music.
Does he?
If there is such a man that ever lived
that could be an example of the true expression and beauty of music, it was Art Tatum. You know?
Yes.
And I say that with all humility and humble respect that you would have for the Lord himself.
Yes. How did you meet him? You heard him play.

I heard Art Tatum as the other people heard him, playing as I said in these jam sessions. All musicians at that time liked to play jazz music played every chance they got. Any place there was a piano, a piano player sat down and played, and some other guys joined him, and they all kinds of places where it was known to be a headquarters for musicians to have these jam sessions. And Art Tatum was at that. Not only that, but I lived with a very, very wonderful man and his wife who always had these little private parties. Now these were different than house rent parties, these were personal parties given by this man who was a businessman. And he loved music, and he loved musicians and entertainers. All the people went to his house. His name was Sonny Howard.
One of the finest gentlemen I ever met in my life, you know.
Out here in Los Angeles.
Right, in Los Angeles.
Right.

And the man became like a father to me, a brother. And I stayed at his house, and this is where Art Tatum and all of the great musicians, Nat Cole, Eddie Beal Bill, another fine pianist, all -- everybody came there every night for these little private parties that he had for people. It was just -- this was -- because this was where everyone could come and relax and have a few drinks, and the musicians felt that they were in their own home, in their own society, and everybody felt like playing because there wasn't anybody in there that didn't understand it. And they were playing for their own people --
No drags.
Ahh, I didn't know you knew what that word meant.
There are too many drags not to know the word.
No, some people won't know how to interpret that, so we'll keep that for our secret.
[PAUSE]
These sessions that Sonny Howard's, which must have been very marvelous, what else -- who else came to them, and did you make up a friendship with Art Tatum at that time?
Very definitely. In fact this has to be the most serious point of my career, and where I really got the

right kind of guidance from Art Tatum as well as many others, particularly Art Tatum. As I said, in this house, these professionals who were then successful people, came there and played every night. Art Tatum just happened to be the star, and the fact of the matter is Art would sit around and drink a little beer and talk. He was very intellectual, very kind gentleman. And most all of the other pianists would come in and play. King Cole would come in and play and he'd sing. And a fine pianist by the name of Eddie Beale. He would play. And any other pianist who came in and felt like playing played.

I played occasionally although I was a little bit ashamed to follow these men. Occasionally before they came I would have enough nerve to sit down and play, because my friend encouraged me, and they all were very encouraging. But I got to know Art Tatum there briefly at the house, and then I remember one time I was playing in a club where they had these jam sessions and I didn't know the chord changes to the "Sweet Lorraine". As I said at this time I was still studying and really learning, you know, these chord progressions and changes, which is the basics of playing jazz music or any ad lib music. You must know the chord progressions, and I didn't know this at that time.
I was very, very studiously learning these songs, and learning progressions and I was sitting there playing one

night, alone, or with a drummer, or some one or two musicians, at this jam session, and I was trying to play 'Sweet Lorraine,' and I was playing it to the best of my ability, which wasn't correct, very evidently. And I got this voice behind me which I recognized to be Art Tatum. It was the most frightening thing I'd ever heard in my life, when it first happened. He said, oh, Charlie, that's not the way it goes, (let me show you.) He sort of suggested that I slide over and he sat down and he showed me how to play 'Sweet Lorraine' in the chord progressions, and showed me how to learn to play progressions on the piano.

Now, this is something that -- a rare occasion that a man so great and so wonderful would take the time. You know, like a lot of guys would either make gesture of it or try to make a fool or something like that, or embarrass you by it. You know, but the man was just so gentle and kind, and he showed me why I was wrong and showed me how to play it right. And from then on I learned many things from Art Tatum. Unfortunately I didn't ever get to be as closest friends [at home,] although just before he died, in the act of actually becoming close to Art Tatum --
Sir Charles, what developed over that time, living there at Sonny Howard Howell's, and benefitting by those marvellous sessions. (inaudible). What came of that, what came after that?
Well, directly -- my contact with like musicians, and King Cole, and other people, spread the word

around about my being a young musician who was interested in music. And through this reputation and contact I referred to Lionel Hampton, and with joined joined Lionel's band with Lionel in California for about a year. And the country (inaudible) a short time and went onto New York.
No, I wanted to ask, by chance, was T-Bone (inaudible) joined the band then?
T-bone?
Yes.
No, T-bone wasn't in that band, in fact I didn't even know T-bone had played with Lionel Hampton. No, I was with Lionel's first band when -- after he left Benny Goodman.
Right. It was later on that --
Yes, this was 1940.
1940, yes, right.
Yes.
And who was in Hamp's band?
There was quite a number of musicians.
Who wasn't.

Well, first of all as I said, number one, the main reason why I was recommended to Lionel was because Lionel had made some very famous records with King Cole, specifically 'Jack the Bellboy' and a couple other things which were really terrific hits. And he wanted King Cole to

play with him, and his entire trio as part of the rhythm section. But King Cole refused to give up his musician because he had faith in himself. And it was through the recommendation of King Cole, who knew about my ability, that he recommended me to Lionel Hampton.

In fact, another thing that happened during that time. They had a street parade once with bands, bands that participated in a street parade including Jimmy Lumsford and some other band. I think it was a band, it might have been organized by the musician's union, 767. But it was like two bands playing together. And King Cole and I were contracted to write the music for this arrangements for this band, and that's how King Cole and I became close in writing this music and going around jamming at night. I learned a lot from King Cole too.
Did you?

So he recommended me to Lionel Hampton, and I joined his band after he left Benny Goodman. Well, in that band was -- well, you know, Illinois Jacquet who I later on played with, that song 'Robin's Nest.' And Marshall Royal, saxophonist and clarinetist. He played violin. Do you want to know the name of that band?
I'd like to.
Ray Perry from Boston. He played violin and guitar -- violin and alto saxophone. And Irving
Nashby, also was from Boston. Guitar player
(Inaudible).

Played guitar. And Vernon Alley was the bass player from San Francisco, and Lee Young, Lester Young's brother was a drummer. He was later replaced by Shadow Wilson in Chicago. And we had -- I don't remember all the players but as I said there was this -- Fred Beckett was in the band, the trombone player, and it was some other player, trombone player that used to do comedy with Lionel Hampton called Sloane. He was a little fella from Texas somewhere. And then there was Dexter Gordon.
I was just going to say was there another tenor saxophone player.
Dexter Gordon was in the band.
Right.
And there was Jack McVez. He played--
Tenor.
-- baritone saxophone, baritone and alto.
Oh.

And he was a very good alto player too and he played very good baritone. He had a very good sound like Harry Carney, you know. And the fact of the matter is that might be a good cue for Mr. Ellington to replace Harry Carney. Jack MacVez would be a good replacement, I'm sure.

That'll cost you another -- oh, let's be nice. But Jack MacVey has a big sound like Harry Carney, the baritone. And he was a very good alto player with a beautiful tone. And he also played tenor too, but he played tenor mostly lately, after that.
Yes.
I can't remember all of the players but --
No, but surely that was the best band that you'd played with to that point, wasn't it? I mean, as far as having star musicians, stellar musicians?
Oh, no doubt. This was an all star band, it was definitely an all star band. All of the musicians were capable.
What did you feel about Hamp?
What did I feel about Hamp?
Yeah.

To me it was the greatest thrill I ever had in my life, because I just -- I thought Lionel Hampton was one of the most talented musicians I'd ever seen in my life, and I was just flabbergasted to play with. In fact I was so nervous that I couldn't play, hardly, because -- of course, you know, Lionel used to like play both ends of the piano and you never knew which end he was going to get on.
Yeah, right.

And then he did so many things, I mean there was so much going on. Actually, I just considered myself very lucky to be with so many fine musicians, and I really just enjoyed every minute of it. You know.
Yes.

And we later on went to Chicago and played in the Grand Terrace for a while, and that's where I decided --I thought I wanted to go on my own, because I didn't get a chance to play enough in the big band, and there were several things I didn't like about the business of the band. And I got sick also, I had a little summer pneumonia there and I just wasn't too happy.
Right.
And I decided to go on to New York on my own, I went to Buffalo, New York first and then I finally went on to New York.
Right. One other thing I'd like to ask you about Hamp. Hamp's talents for improvisation and his knowledge of chord progressions and what not, I mean he's an extremely experienced musician, is he not?

Well, I always said, and I say this still now, I have never -- I've played with all the musicians that you can name, practically, that were jazz musicians in my life time, and I've never played with anyone more talented on the drums or the vibraphones than Lionel. And of course

he can play that piano with those two fingers, and get a lot of music out of it. And he's -- the man is incredible, he's just a natural born genius as a player, as a player. There's no doubt in my mind, as Dan -- and I would also have to say that I learned more from him than I had from anyone else as far as playing music is because before that I had been primarily an arranger.
Yes.
And I hadn't concentrated on band playing with rhythm sections. I had been a good solo player of parties, but I had never been exposed to the real hardcore jazz, you see.
Right.

And this is where I really got that foundation. And Lionel -- as I said, the man is a genius, is just -- he gets so much out of what he does, it's unbelievable how that man can play the drums and the vibraphones, as I said. My personal opinion is there's no one can top him. He is a marvelous musician.
Yes.
He is.
He's so integrated with his band, isn't he? I mean, he sets off his band in such a marvelous way, doesn't he?
Well, Lionel in so many ways is like a

little boy, which is very good. I think a person who can keep these feelings as a young person, have these young ideas and doesn't get too wrapped up in themselves, too serious, I think is an asset. And that's the thing that keeps Lionel young and agile. The man has the mind -- he keeps himself young in spirit. He's always enjoys what he's doing.
Right.
Completely. And that's one of his attributes.
Yes. The well springs are there. It isn't put on or it isn't a front.
As well as talent.
(Tape 5)
Sir Charles, when you were with Lionel and you were playing the Grand Terrace, you made a record session at that time, didn't you?

Yes, we made a very important record session there, to me, because it was my first professional recording, and it was done with Lionel, with a small group of musicians which included first Lee Young. I believe Lee Young was on some of the records on the drums. You can look this up but also Shadow Wilson came in the band later.
Yes.
But the basic group was made up of Marshall Royal who played clarinet on the date, and Ray Perry

played violin, and some alto. But primarily Marshall played the clarinet and Ray Perry played the violin, and there was Vernon Alley, the bass player, he was on those records. He hadn't been replaced yet, and there was Lionel on the vibes, and Irving Ashby on guitar, and myself on piano.

And one of those dates was a trumpet player who later on left the group. Karl George. He was a very, very fine first trumpet player with a beautiful tone, who had played with Teddy Wilson's very fine, big band. And he had a beautiful sound. He was instrumental --
First man.

First trumpet. He was very instrumental in making that band sound beautiful, and together, because he was an excellent first trumpet player, you know. So that was very, very important to me, although I don't think the records turned out as well as Lionel would have liked them to, and I'm sure they weren't as good as the records he had already made with the more experienced musicians. Because Lionel had already made a lot of records with great musicians and including like I said King Cole and some of Benny Goodman's side men, and Teddy Wilson. And I can understand this.
Did you write some arrangements for Hamp's band when he was at the Terrace, or around that time?
Yes, I did, in fact I spent most of my time in that band writing arrangements because as I said

there really wasn't much for me to play. There was a lot of players in the band, and Lionel featured himself mostly playing the piano, vibraphone, the drums, and he had a little act he did with the saxophone player and the trombone player. And he had a battle of music going with the two tenors, the Illinois Jacquet and Dexter Gordon. So he had pretty much a thing set for his bands.
So I concentrated on writing music, for the band, and I wrote quite a few arrangements for the band, and as I said. But I became --
Can you remember what ones they were?

Oh, not really. I don't remember that well, the details of everything that I wrote. I wrote practically everything that you can mentioned with that would swing. I had a lot of original material, and I just tried to write everything that came into my head, get the experience of writing, take advantage of all these fine musicians that could play the music that I wrote. Because previous to that, the other bands that I'd been in, they had to rehearse a long time, they very often didn't play the music well.

But here for the first time I had musicians who could read well and interpret the music and play it, and so I do remember one song in particular I wrote. An original called "Train Time Dorraine." But any way, as I said, I finally left the band and went on -- I decided that I should try to do

something on my own, and I decided to go to New York. And I stopped over in Buffalo where I played with a group of musicians there. George Clark who had been with Stuff Smith, the violinist. In fact I had heard him, they had a great small band, one of the finest small bands I'd ever heard in my life. But they were mainly entertainers also, but they played good music. George Clark played tenor saxophone, and Jonah Jones played the trumpet. He was in that band. And they were quite something. Stuff Smith was a genius on the violin, and--
He had perfect pitch too.
Oh, yeah, he was a great entertainer and great player, and oh, they were really great. I enjoyed their music many times when they were playing.
Was Cozy with them?
Cozy Cole was a drummer, yes.
Yes.

So any way I spent a little time around Buffalo, and I played with some of the musicians who I had played with with Omaha, Nebraska, in Omaha, Nebraska, including that drummer Debo Mills. We played out there at a place called [Bardos.] They had a lot of shows, and we played these shows with this six piece band, and tried to play our little jazz music inbetween, for $22.00 a week. You know.
But I finally went on to New York, and it was there that I was inspired by other great piano players like Pete

Johnson and Albert Ammons became very influential in my life, and they taught me the boogie-woogie style. And Pete Johnson was a very warm human being. And he and Albert Ammons both. And the fact of the matter is the way I went to New York was I was sent to play with Lester Young, who was my real love. Actually Lester Young was my real love, because I like to play tenor too.
Really?
Yes, I always liked to play tenor.
I didn't know that.

Well it was hard on the teeth, and of course then I'd already established myself as a piano player, and it wasn't really the time to devote to it. And then you know, you can't learn everything at once, but I always loved Lester Young, and really I tried to pattern my playing after Lester Young on the piano, and that's what really established my original style of playing until, as I said, met Art Tatum who taught me more about the piano itself, you know.
But I was sent to come to play with Lester Young --
Did Lester send for you then?
I don't know. I'm sure --
Whoever.
-- Lester -- he -- they had told him -- I'm sure they had asked him probably some opinion about me. (I knew him. He must have knew about it.) Sure, of course. I met him in
Omaha, he knew what I did, and I'm sure that he wouldn't agree to have someone play who he didn't particularly like it.
Of course not.
And the fact of the matter is he's the one who named me Sir Charles, incidentally.
How?
How do you like that?
I love it.

In fact I would have to say, with all sincerity, Lester Young loved me as a piano player, as a musician, as a guy. As I said because I met him earlier in Omaha, Nebraska when I first started, he knew me from the beginning and he knew my interest in music, and he knew I was really serious about music, and that I liked his music, and his style, and I liked him. And he was just beautiful.
He named Billie Lady Day and he named you Sir Charles.

Yes, he was quite capable -- he always was naming people. In fact the way I got the name, when I got to New York they were playing in the famous Cafe Society, which was the most high class jazz night club in the world as has ever been. And of course later on Billy Berg had one too in Hollywood, and I came there with Coleman Hawkins later. But this was really an exciting place, a wonderful -- a very beautiful night club, and they had the top entertainment in

the world. At the time that I was playing there they featured such artists as Hazel Scott. Hazel Scott was very often featured there as a solo performer. She played alone and with a trio. And as I said they had this Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons, they played inbetween.
And then our band played and the band played for shows, you know. And so --
It was Lee and Lester, yourself and who else?

Well, actually it was Lee and Lester's band, and in the band was featured Red Callendar. Very wonderful bass who you know of. He's made a lot of records with Art Tatum, in fact he was perhaps one of Art Tatum's favorite basses, Red Callendar. Beautiful human being. Very, very wonderful musician, friend of mine. He was playing the bass, and there was another guitarist. Oh, I'll have to research his name, it'll come to me maybe, in a few minutes.

And there was a trumpet player by the name of Paul Campbell who came from St. Louis. He had played with some of the midwestern bands in St. Louis. And there was another tenor player named Bumps Myers.
Oh, and yes, from here, from L. A.
Yes.
Wonderful tenor player.
Yes, he was a good tenor player. It
was a good band.
I didn't realize that he was in that. He was in that band with Lester?
Yes, yes, yes.
He played Hawk style in a sense, didn't he?
No, not really.
No?
Bumps -- I don't know how to describe his --
Or Buddy's style?

No, Bumps really had a style of his own, in a way. Bumps was -- I don't know how to describe his style but I think he had his own little personality, you know, and he was a nice person too, and it was quite interesting to see the way that Lester accepted having another tenor player in his small band. It was only actually two horns.
Yes.
Three horns.
Three, with the trumpet, yes.

And the other horn being a tenor. Usually they would have an alto player, but see there again you get into the love and warmth of jazz. I can really say -- I didn't know, I wasn't there when the band organized, but it had to be because of his personality and warmth that he
was hired in the band. Because normally they would want to have a contrast and use an alto sax.
Right.

But any way, it was a nice band, and we stayed in there -- I think I was in there about 26 weeks or whatever, the termination of the engagement was. And the band sort of disbanded, and I stayed in New York.

Well, before you get off that I want to ask you more, because I never heard Lester with his own group there, and Lester being the wonderful and extraordinary personality that he was how was he as a sort of a leader, I mean I take it that Lester was the man, not Lee -- I mean, did Lester -- did he front the band and run the band, or did he -- well, you tell me what happened?

Well, that's a hard question to answer except I'd like to maybe use an unusual way to describe the way Lester ran the band. Lester led the band with his eyes. He hardly said anything except hey baby, or you know, everything that Lester had to say usually was complimentary. You know. And he had nothing to say hardly at all except through his horn, but you could look at his eyes and tell what he was thinking if you were with him.
Now, I would say actually most of the you might say the discipline or any words which were spoken, which were very few, perhaps, were done by his brother Lee, who was very

business oriented. He was more of a businessman, you know. And Lester strictly was a jazz player, but -- now by no means am I saying that Lester did not lead the band, because he did lead the band. But you see in a good band like that, you really don't necessarily need a leader because all the men understand what's happening, and as I said, you just -- a guy would call a number and you say -- you call the number, you name the tune or you call it by number, or you whisper or you say -- or before you get on the bandstand, well we're going to play such and such and such a thing. So when you get up on the bandstand you know what's happening and everybody's just waiting for the beat to start.
Who beat off?

Well, as I said, I don't remember precisely, but I think Lee actually probably counted for a lot of the tunes, and then some was done by Lester. But there is no doubt that it was Lester's band, you know, really.
Yes.

Lester was the leader, there's no question about it. I mean, like every band, some bands who have leaders, sometimes they have somebody else in the band who maybe starts off certain pieces or does a few things like that. But, you know, as a man or as a professional performer, everyone recognizes who the leader is, and there was no question about it that Lester was the leader of the band because he was the great jazz player, and he was the man that people really
came to hear as the leader.
Yes, of course.

But he wasn't the type of person that-- he didn't care if people knew who -- he wasn't interested in being known as the leader, because he was a jazz player who played his horn for the love of it and he just played. And he never acted as a leader, he just played.
I want to ask you. You said you played back with the shows, am I right,or back of the -- an act or two?

Yes. Well, when I say shows, that can be very deceiving. See a show could mean anything from one group to several groups, and in this particular place it was a very small place and they used to have, as I said, name acts; mainly the show consisted of the band and the piano duo of Pete Johnson, Albert Ammons, and they had a singer. You know, sometimes it would be a singer with her own accompanist, or it would be a singer who would come -- some of them were comedians. I don't remember their names, you know.
Yes.
I never did like to accompany singers myself, you know.
No.
Personally. I did a few things with
Billie Holliday but I was like -- somewhat like Lester in my strict love for jazz.
Yes.

I was always a guy that liked to play jazz. We wanted to play jazz. And we didn't mind playing for singers, really, who we thought were good. Like Billie Holliday was always a pleasure to play with, if she was feeling well, and, you know -- but you know, it just was a thing you did as a chore.
I know, I know.
When you played for someone else, because we wanted to play for ourselves.
I know. The reason really I asked you, in a way,was that because I mean Lester was not a great man for chores, you know --
Right.
-- if he could possibly --
Well, most of -- as I said, was so short.
Yes.

The band had very little to play for the singers, because usually as I said they had their own piano player, or something like that, or like, you know, like Lester maybe didn't play the whole set, you know, like maybe the rhythm section or something like that. It was very short.
Like when I say show -- see, the two piano players, they didn't need anybody, they played alone.
That's right.

You know. Or they played with the drums. If they played the drums, then just the drums. Because they didn't need anybody, they could play -- they made enough rhythm with the two pianos to last a long time.
Yes.
And in fact it was through their friendship that I learned how to play the authentic boogie-woogie style of playing, which you know --
Through Pete or --
Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons, yes.
Yes.

And naturally in the process I heard Albert talk about this son of his who he expected to be a great jazz tenor player, and I didn't even know where he was, I hadn't heard of him before. And then I looked up several years later and I found out what he was talking about, because his son turned out to be one of the finest jazz players in the world, Gene Ammons.
Yes.
And he started playing with bands like Woody Herman and was featured as a great player. He was -- his father was right.
Yes,yes.

So any way I spent that time there with Lester Young and all these things were very enjoyable. Would you believe it, after the band disbanded, there was no more work for the band, and I think Lee perhaps went back to California, and I think Lester got took a vacation or something, and we didn't have anything to do so Red Calendar formed a trio with me and the guitar player, you know.
Can't you remember that guitar player's name yet?
No, I can't. It's too bad too.
I'll ---
It's too bad too because I have a picture here of that band I brought along for you to see, which I'll show you at the first opportunity that I get, if I can find it.
Good, good.
I guess maybe I left it someplace else.
Well as a matter of fact it's not serious because it's -- you know, it's (inaudible) available.
Louis [Gonzalez], that's his name. His name is Louis [Gonzalez.]
Oh.
I'm sure. Louis Gonzalez, yes.
Very good --
You and) calendar. (Red Calendar.
Red Calendar.
Yes.
Isn't that marvelous.

We played a few jobs booked out of New York. We had singing, entertaining type of trio, similar to King Cole's group, which was very popular during those days in the small clubs. We played and we had little singing arrangements where we sang in unison mostly.
Really?

And harmony. Yes, we all wrote these little arrangements, yes, yes. A very, very nice trio. But it's always been a problem to get bookings, and so we didn't last too long, and Red went back to California and I stayed in New York and was lucky enough to sort of do some things on my own. I played with a lot of musicians around New York and made some records on my own.

Yes, I mean I think you were rather exceptional. I mean,most musicians have a hard time getting to New York, and have a hard time surviving right away. I mean, you -- to come in with Lester was a very marvelous way to be introduced into New York, wasn't it?
Yes, it was. Well, the fact of the matter is I'll tell you the strange thing about it is I was influenced to come there because of my love for music strictly,

strictly music love. Because in those days the money was very little, in fact I was making $75.00 a week playing with George Clarke Carr, and I was influenced to come to join Lester Young for $55.00 a month -- a week.
Oh, fancy that that's (inaudible). Yes.
That seems almost unreal now.
It does seem unreal, it really does.
You know, but I didn't really go for the money because I went for $20.00 less.
That's right, you did indeed.
But it was --
You did it to be with Lester, to join Lester.

Right, it was my love for the music. And of course I wanted to go to New York too because it was a jazz mecca, and I had very -- well, a lot of people who were very kind to me, you know, in my association in New York.
Well, who became your special friends in New York at that time?
Oh, when I say friends. (friends) (really)
Musicians I meant.

I met a lot of people in the business, you know many -- all the musicians, as I said, that I played with, I got to know them. I played with Hot Lips Page and Roy Eldridge and oh, many other musicians played there. Don
Was and you know.
Yes.
In fact I was more or less a utility piano player on 52nd Street.
On 52nd Street was so busy then.
Yes.
So big. And of course a pianist who could fall right in with everybody, you know --
Yes.
-- that --
In fact this is when I met Coleman Hawkins during that period.
I was just going to say.
Later on, yes. And to me -- as I said, my whole life was spent studying music with these great artists, and I was learning all the time.

I'd like to -- perhaps we're digressing a little bit, but while we're speaking of Hawk I'd like to have you speak more about Hawk because he and Lester of course were the two greats, and of course were very different styles. Hawk too was a man that was -- had great depth as far as chord progressions and what not was concerned, harmonics and so on. Correct?
Definitely. In fact --
He was an adventurer, a musical adven-

turer, wasn't he? I refer to Coleman Hawkins as a college of music, jazz music, any kind of music, jazz music in particular. Because that's the way -- but you can remember that I've met people like Art Tatum, and I put Coleman Hawkins in the same category. These people were what you call the ultimate in teachers of music. If anyone had any kind of ear at all, had any kind of knowledge, and was interested at all in learning, you had to learn something from these people. And as I said, this was my primary reason for associating with these people as well as loving to listen to them I was intent on learning from them.

And as I said, Coleman Hawkins turned out to be a college of music for me, because he was involved in the highest form of progressions and music interpretation that there was around in those days. And he was considered to be one of the fathers of all times of this business (of) jazz music, you know. He had gone to Europe and on the strength of his ability he had created a reputation for himself that was incomparable. And he came back to the states in the midst of controversy about some of the young players like Don Byas or other players like Lester Young who they wanted to know whether he had lost his competitive spirit, or whether he had lost his inspiration, his ability to play. And he came back and proved it, that he was still one of the greats in the field of music. Although

like I said in my opinion I've always liked all of these musicians and I don't like to categorize musicians, but it's only natural that you compare them. And I always considered Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins to be the two leaders of the tenor saxophone playing, you know.

And they had entirely different styles, but as I said, Coleman Hawkins was more of a teacher, because he'd sit down to the piano and show you what chord progressions he wanted, and he dealt in these chord progressions and he's a great listener of classical music. And he had expensive equipment in his -- he was one of the first people I remember hearing in New York who had an expensive hi-fi equipment when it first came out, you know. And this type of thing. He had an expensive baby grand piano in his apartment. He had the things necessary and to show another musician what was happening in this field of music. And he could express it, he could play it, and he could teach it, and he knew what he was doing, and he had the depth that was -- just incomparable. Like ballads. ballots. You know, the man could play a ballad like Art Tatum played on the piano, and he could invert these chords and he could get so much expression in them, you know. So I always considered Coleman Hawkins like a college of music, and my playing with him was I'd say one of the highlights of my life. I played with him in New York, and we made some

records, in New York, and we travelled -- toured the country, a brief tour of the midwestern states, and on to California where we played in Billy Berg's famous jazz club. And we were considered to be one of the first organized groups to play the type of music that we were playing, which was considered to be modern, although it really wasn't that modern in the sense, but that's the way they referred to it.

It was during the time that the writers were beginning to categorize music and musicians, you know, as to what they were playing. And they very often referred to the music as bebop or rebop. And would you believe it, ironically it came because the last note they played, that the drums and the horns played rebop, on maybe one or two songs. So they said rebop, you know.
Yes.

But it wasn't that at all, it was just the guys were playing music and they had different endings -- you know, people that would write about music and don't always know how to name it. They only know how to describe it, which is understandable. You know.

Yes. I think it was doubly remarkable in a way in that as you say when he came back from Europe people were waiting to see what could he do with what had gone on while he was away, and so on. I mean, there was Dizzy and Charlie Parker and so on, and it was so remarkable that
Hawk took all that had been done, and not only assimilated it but built on it. Correct?

Well, I'd have to correct you on that in this sense. You said there was Charlie Barker and this Dizzy Gillespie. That is wrong in this respect. These people were inspired by Coleman Hawkins, believe it or not, and Art Tatum.
I [knew of him.]

Coleman Hawkins came back and called it 'Body and Soul', which I know was definitely done as early as '39. Right? Now, it was through that record that everybody recognized that Coleman Hawkins was a leader of jazz saxophonists and musicians, with a modern sense. Now it was through this that these people like you're talking about, like Dizzy Gillespie, Charles Parker, who were just starting out on their own, they were inspired by him.
Yes.
Do you understand that?
Oh, I do understand that.
Do you understand what I mean?
Yes.
And now they embellished --
He preceeded them by quite a bit.
Right.
Quite a time.
Right.
Benny Carter. I mean, Benny Carter enjoyed joined the same status.

Right, right, that's what I'm talking about. And Benny Carter is also another school of jazz music or music period. He's a genius, the man's a genius. Well, this is what I'm saying. So actually this was really the man that inspired the musicians who became involved in the new music that they now are experimenting with.
Yes.
To be kind with my words.
Right, right.
You know?
One thing I want to ask you and didn't ask you was who was in that -- who was in the band with Hawk when you were in that band? Who else was in that band? Can you remember? Who was the drummer?

A very sensitive, one of the most sensitive musical drummers that I ever played with. His name was Denzil Denzer Best. And there was this great bass player who I told you about who I'd played with and met earlier in my life in Minnesota, Minneapolis, Minnesota. Oscar Pettiford.
Yes.
Who as I said there was quite some controversy about who was the greater player. He or Jimmy
Blanton.
Yes.

It just so happened that Jimmy Blanton was featured with Duke Ellington under the best circumstances he was able -- he got before the public in such a fashion. So Pettifort had a little hard time establishing himself on his own, you see. But Oscar Pettiford was a genius, in his own right, on the bass.
And after all Duke recognized it afterwards any way, not that he didn't recognize it in the beginning, but I mean he also showcased Oscar Pettiford afterwards.

Yes, yes. Well, as a matter of choice at the time he hired Jimmy Blanton of course and then you'd have to say -- in comparing them I would have to say that Jimmy Blanton had the real genius qualities and the class and all of these other things, plus he was a quiet type of person who I think was able to express himself musically a little better than Oscar who was more of a jolly talkable type of fella, you know.
Yes.
But the main thing I wanted to speak about about this group was that it was a very musical group and it was very inventive. Everybody in the band was a writer, you know. Denzil Best wrote music.
Did he?
And we played some of his music. McGhee And then there was Howard McGee, a very, very fine trumpet player.
Oh, yes, yes.

Unfortunately he had some bad luck, physical handicaps, and later on he -- well, the band didn't stay together too long either. We came to Hollywood and we played Billy Berg's for a short period, and then we made this picture that featured our band in a moving picture that was made with Noah Beery Jr., and some other people. I think the name of the picture was the "Crimson Canary Murder Case".
Oh.
And we had a scene in there playing in a jazz club.
Oh. Have you ever seen it since?
Yes, I saw it in New York when it first came out, you know. It wasn't a very good picture, but it was exciting to see myself bow in the picture.
Yes. It must have been a very good musical sequence too, wasn't it.

Some of the music was good, but it wasn't the best because unfortunately because of the technical-ities in those days of the -- the music was recorded at one time, and you had to pretend you were playing, and some of the

things that weren't compatible to the feeling of jazz, some of the recordings didn't come off too good. But there were also some very good ones. Some of the ones that I'm very proud to have been on, some of my favorite recordings that I've made were made on those Capitol Albums that were made during that time. It was called "Hollywood Stampede".
Oh?

Particularly the ballads. I thought they were very good. We recorded "April in Paris", which was over recorded after that in many fashions, but it was later made famous by Bill Davis on the organ and Count Basie. One More Time.
Yes, I remember.

"April in Paris" arrangement. But we had a beautiful arrangement that went on that, featuring Coleman Hawkins on those recordings of Capitol. And I had a song also that I had a little something to do with during that time which brought out my first solo identification, believe it or not, in that band. It's the first time that I came to be known as a solo player with my own style, which brought out this style of playing that I had, which was my own, and later on become recognized as me. And that was a piece called "Stuffy" Stuffing.
Yes, I think I remember that. That was an up tempo, wasn't it?
Medium tempo. (Humming).
That's right, that's it. That was your number too?
(Humming).
Right. Wonderful number, wonderful number.
That was -- I was ---
Beautiful tempo for Hawk.

Yes,well, see, these are the kind of things -- these kind of creations,musicians -- we got these things together as a group. Maybe I would have an idea, and Coleman Hawkins would have an idea, we'd get it together and make a piece out of it, see. And of course in some cases where it was done as a group the leader would get credit for being a composer, and so forth and so on, so forth. And I didn't get any credit for it, in fact I didn't consider myself as being the author of that piece, but we all had something to do with making it a hit. And it was one of the famous records out of that album.
Yes, yes.
In fact it was the most famous, I believe, of those recordings which later became almost like a theme song to Coleman and Roy Eldridge, who loved to play that song.
Right, right.
And I was very flattered that they used to play my solo together.
Yes. Really, did they?
I'd like to hum it for you now.
Do hum it.
The first solo I played that I was identified with as a jazz player --
By all means,
-- that they had played until his death. My solo went like this. (Humming).
And the first time I was able to establish my identity as a jazz player as a soloist, believe it or not. And that was I think 1945.
Is that right?
That's right.
Boy, that's a lot of --
Then I later on went from there and I wrote a lot of original songs for the band. I had many -- one called 'Ladies Lullaby', which I wrote as a dedication to Lady Day, Billie Holiday.
Yes.
And some other things that I did with the band.
Did that get any lyrics, 'Ladies Lullaby'?
No, no, it never got even popular.

In fact we scuffled through that, that's one of the things that didn't come off too good. We did that for another album, another recording company in New York before we went on tour. But what I'm saying, it was during this period I had all this experience with Coleman Hawkins and I was learning. And of course I forgot to tell you about the period in Buffalo before I came to New York, which was my most exciting period in writing music, you know. We talked about everything but that.

And before I came to join Lester Young in New York I had written for a number of bands, you know, from time to time, and I had written some things for Count Basie that he liked very much. Because at that time Count Basie was looking for all kinds of music to be played, because, you know, Basie had a lot of ideas but he didn't have time to write them and he always got other people to write them. And because of this warm relationship I had with Count Basie, who I told you knew me when I was a kid, in Colorado Springs, when he was with Bus Moten, because of that relationship and the connection I had with Joe Jones and Lester Young playing with them, the other guys who heard about me writing arrangements with Nat Towles Fells and these other people, Count Basie made me an offer to join his band as an arranger, a regular arranger.
Because I finally put all this knowledge together in my writing that I had picked up, and I finally learned how to write, and while I'm saying this, out I forgot all about the
time before I left with Lionel Hampton that I had spent as a copyist for Fletcher Henderson, the famous arranger who wrote for Benny Goodman. You know?
You were a copyist. When?

I copied music for Benny Goodman when he was writing -- for Fletcher Henderson when he was writing for Benny Goodman. He was living in the Dunbar Hotel, and he is the one that showed me in about two or three days what I'd been trying to learn in four or five years. How to voice properly for orchestration. I had tried to learn by listening, I had listened to Count Basie's band, all these other writers who had this -- they had different styles, and it was about this time they came out with the famous Schillinger system of writing, which I had actually been using all the time, only I hadn't been doing it mathematically. The Schillinger has to do with mathematics of where the note is supposed to be. It's very mechanical. I don't like it myself, personally. You know, it has no feeling to it, it's all mechanical.
You know, in other words you know that this note is supposed to be in the chord --
[From the book.]
(Inaudible).
And you know it's supposed to be played at a certain time, if that's a chord there, you know.
Yes, yes.
Like one, two, three, four, six, and
eight, and you know. But Fletcher Henderson is one that taught me.
When you say you learned from Smack, I'm interested to know did Smack actually give you a little help or did you pick it up right out of what you were copying there?
Well, first of all let's clarify who Smack was.
Oh, of course.
A lot of people won't know. That was a nickname for Smack, you know, like my name is Sir Charles.
Exactly.
And before I forget it -- I told you Lester Young gave me the name of Sir Charles.
Yes.

There were three Charleses working in Cafe Society where I told you we were playing. And like they had a phone in the back where the bandstand was, and the rest rooms and the dressing rooms in that area. So when they'd call for Charles one of the guys who ran the elevator's name was Charles, my name was Charles, and another Charles. Right?
Right.

So nobody knew who it was, and of course I for some reason or another got most of the calls, and so Lester Young Johnson said, 'listen, we've got to get this thing straightened out.' He said, 'listen, my man said you look like
royalty any way, you should have a name so we can identify you he said. Baby, we're going to call you Sir Charles, you know. And that's where I got the name.
Well, so getting back to -- you know --
That's very nice,
Yes (inaudible).
Count Basie said I joined the royalty family, which I considered an honor.
Yes.
You know. It's a gimmick, really, one of those things.
It's nice, it's nice.

I had one booking agent tell me once in New York, the late Billy Show, when I first went there he said, Sir Charles, you've got to have gimmicks. Always carry a brief case in your hand and have a big cigar and wear a derby. He wanted me to do like Willie the Lion. I didn't think that was too original, so I thought I would stick with my music.
(inaudible).
Henderson's
But any way, that was Fletcher Henderson's nickname, Smack.
Yes.
As you said. Yes, well he was also -- as I've told you, a lot of these great musicians -- you'd be surprised, if they liked you they would tell you things, which

was like getting free information that would cost you a million dollars or you would have to go to school for for years to learn. And like I said, in a very short time Fletcher Henderson straightened me out on how to voice music which I had been trying to use my original ideas and things I'd heard other guys do which seemed to make a band sound bigger, you know. But it was a more complicated way of doing it. Fletcher Henderson showed me the simple way of doing it, which was very simple. Just basic fundamentals of music, just like any athletic sports.

Like you hear the basketball players in particular talk about -- or golfers. They always talk about coming back to the basic principles and fundamentals of the sport, you know. If it's basketball they come back to the basic fundamentals of their game, like the Boston Celtics, if we may go into this a little deeper, they have their fast running breaks and they work a team to death fast, and they pass and they're tricky and they can shoot well, you know. They put all that together when they find themselves frustrated. The same way with a golfer. When he finds himself hitting a ball in the woods instead of trying to hit it long and far, he comes back to try and hit it straight and in the middle, and putting feeling in his wrist, and chipping at the ball so he can one-putt, you know, things of that sort. That's what I mean by the basic fundamentals.
Yes.

Yes, as I said, Fletcher Henderson taught me those basic fundamentals, and he did it as an extra bonus payment for me for copying his music that he needed very badly and quickly. Because he was writing for Benny Goodman when he was playing in the Coconut Grove, Ambassador Hotel, and you know, many times they'd have to change the copyist arrangement around and he needed a quick copies, like, you know, that was able to do this. And you know, as payment to me and you know, as a friendly gesture he showed me what he could show me, which was really appreciated by me. And as I said, through this knowledge that I learned then I was able to write these arrangements later for bands like Count Basie, and which was flattering to me. And -- but I didn't want to travel under those circumstances, because I didn't think I could do justice in writing, being required to write as many as three arrangements a week for a basic salary, of a minimum salary. And so rather than to do a sloppy job, as I saw some of the fellas doing and trying to keep up with this requirement, I decided against it. And in fact I'm sort of happy that I did because I don't think -- I might have missed getting the experience of playing with these great musicians like Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins had I kept into that field of just writing. And I wanted to be a player.
Right
But I hadn't really still gotten enough experience as a player, you know.
Right. It seemed to me there were --(yes, well it -- even that you'd done arrangements for Jimmy Dorsey's band and did you actually arrange for Fletcher's band too?
No.
No.

No, no. I only copied music for Fletcher Henderson for a brief time while he was in town, and the band was at the Coconut Grove. In fact I was trying -- I was hoping that I'd be able to replace him a sa pianist, because as an arranger he wasn't considered to be a very, you know, flowery pianist who was flattering the band. I think Johnny Guarneri had been in the band, who has an excellent pianist, one of my favorites today. But Fletcher was not real-ly loose enough to be a jazz piano player. And Charlie Christian, who then was with Benny Goodman and a friend of mine from the old days in Oklahoma City when I travelled with Nat Towles, was going to try to recommend me to Benny Goodman and get me a shot, an of audition.
But unfortunately Charlie died before he got a chance to introduce me to Benny Goodman and --
What a shame.
Yes.
Teddy was with him then though, wasn't he? Or Jess Stacey was with him too.
No, I think Teddy Wilson had left. See Teddy had left --
Oh, I see.
You know, Lionel and Teddy had left him.
Yes, that's right.
See, this is -- you know, the later period, like around -- this was, I don't know, in the forties some time.
You know, just to go back a minute. You mentioned about Nat Towles. Yes, well Charlie was in that for a time, wasn't he, with Nat Towles' band. Charlie Christian was for a time.
No, Charlie played with --
When you were there.
He played with another band. I can't think of the name, in that neighborhood in Oklahoma. He was from Oklahoma City. There was another band, Alphonso Trent.
[Ralston Brooks.] Oh, Alphonso.
Alphonso Trent.
Right, yes.
The
That was that band.
Right, good. Well, let's get back to right where we are here. Well, you went out to the west coast and with Hawk, and then you were with Lucky Millinder for a while. I didn't realize that. Were you?
Yes. While I was in -- when I first went to New York, this is before this period that we're talking now, this is back when I first went to New York, when I joined Lester Young.
Yes.

Well, in order to earn a living, you know, very often, you know, there wasn't enough work on 52nd Street to keep me working all the time, and I was also putting in my time to join the musician's union. You were required to be in that area for a six month period. And I hadn't joined the union, so in order to join the union I played with Lucky Millinder, to, you know, make a living and put in my time.
I see.
You see.
Right, yes.

And I played with him and I wrote some arrangements for the band and he was kind enough to feature me in the band, when he had musical features. He was more or less an entertaining band which featured singers and high class arrangements. He had jazz arrangements of pieces like
you know, classical, some classical music, and Holiday in Strings was one of them.
Yes.

And he featured me on the piano, and these type of things. He was quite a showman, and he kept good musicians with him all the time. He had one of the best bands around New York, he was considered to be one of the top bands in New York, along with --
Who was in that band, can you remember?
Oh, there's plenty guys. Joe Guy was their trumpet player who later married Billie Holiday, you know about him. Oh, a lot of musicians played them. I could name quite a few of them.
Yes, Tab Smith, wasn't it?
Tab Smith.
Wasn't he in the band?

Yes, he was in the band, but not when I was in there. But he -- Lucky Millinder had the ability to pick musicians, and he tried to get all of the good musicians in his band with him. And he was a good guy to work for, and he was very, very congenial and very flattering to musicians. But I didn't stay with him too long because he wasn't a jazz player, and you know the band wasn't really my particular style, you know. But I stayed with the band --
Yeah. But it helped you through that
period.
Oh, sure, of course. It was a very good job for that time, you know.
That was about 1946. I think sometimes I forget to really pinpoint these years, but then you led a band -- co-led a band with Illinois Jacquet, 1947-48.

Well, during the time I was playing with Coleman Hawkins which was after I played with Lucky Millinder, when I got to California as I said, the bookings sort of petered out and rather than to continue on the road with these uncertainties, I got together with Illinois Jacquet, who we had played together, we had played together with Lionel Hampton, and we organized a band together. We played in San Diego -- San Diego, yes. We played a job in San Diego. It didn't last too long, but we had Henry Coker on trombone and Oscar Pettiford on bass --
Oh.

And his brother, Russell Jacquet on trumpet. But this didn't last too long because we didn't have any bookings and so forth, and I went back to New York and continued on with my association and then we got together again in New York when he later came there, and I collaborated with him in playing and arranging and writing some music, out of which came my composition 'Robin's Nest'. That was in 1947.
Yes.
Right. Well, had you -- I mean, how much recording had you done by then?

Well, by that time then I had already -- I more or less had established myself in the recording field of jazz, with some recordings that I'd done previous to all of these things with Apollo Records. I made my first recordings on my own, with Apollo Record Company. I think this was about 1944, and I made some great arrangements and some great tunes, and recordings, and I had in the band a great personnel with Charlie Parker as one of my side men. Charlie Parker was on alto saxophone, and Dexter Gordon was on tenor saxophone, and Buck Clayton, my old friend and mentor was willing to help me out and he played the trumpet. And I had such great musicians as J. C. Heard on the drums and on some of those recordings I made later I had Osie O.-C. Johnson --
Yes.

And of course as I said these records that I'm talking about now in '44 had -- I had a bass player by the name of Jimmy Butts who was a New York bass player, and I had a guitarist who was with Cab Calloway. And I had a real fine group there. I made some great tunes and --
Many of them were originals, weren't they?
Most of them were originals, most of
all of them were originals. Out of that came a song called "Tune Us In," and Sir Charles -- let's see, "20th Century Blues," and "Street Beat," and -- oh, I can't think of all of them but--
Were you fortunate with your royalties with the publishing company?
Oh, definitely.
Or would you put them with --

Definitely not. In fact I didn't get any money at all. I got paid for the date and I didn't get any money for -- which is a sad part of my life. But unfortunately I wasn't a good businessman and you know, in this business they always tell you you have to make a name for yourself. Even now people are telling me, rather than to offer you a decent salary they tell you that you have to get known, you know, or you have to have a hit records or some-thing.

And unfortunately for me the song that I wrote that was a hit, that wasn't recorded under my name, and it was a controversy about who wrote it because I agreed to give Jacques co-authorship of the song and the copyright, although actually it was my song. And so consequently a lot of people were not aware of the fact that I am the composer of "Robin's Nest," you see.
Yes.
So this was one of those unfortunate
situations.
Yes.

But unfortunately it's just unbelievable how the paper work and the contracts in this business are so badly arranged for the artists, and it's hard to believe now that in these days of 1975 that entertainers are making more money than Babe Ruth made in one week, or in one month, you know.
Yes.

And I'd have to say that they're not necessarily playing good music, you know, without criticizing any of the music that's being played, without being that facetious. You know, but I even had Duke Ellington tell me, and I've read about Fats Waller. Fats Waller sold a lot of his songs for $1.00 or whatever he could get, as you might know. And because of this ignorance of contract agreements, and the influence of these promoters of music and bookers in and around New York, and the lack of having anybody to advise me, unfortunately the contracts that I signed were by no means beneficial to me in any respect. And a lot of the songs that I wrote and recorded in those days was completely out of my hands as far as the benefits of the money is concerned.
Where your royalties were concerned.
And many people have the impression that I should be a wealthy man because of the fact that I made
all of these recordings, but unfortunately I didn't get paid hardly anything for them. And as you know I made some recordings later, also, for Vanguard and Columbia.
I'd like to hear about those Vanguard records.

Well, I made several Vanguard records, some of which were first with a trio, a trio of guitar, bass and drums. They were done with Skeeter Best, a very, very fine guitarist and Aaron Bell, who had played with Duke Ellington bass, and myself on piano. And we later incorporated some other musicians for later sessions, but it was fundamentally the trio session that I recorded first, you know. And I had on there some original songs, also, which I dedicated one of the numbers to my old friend Sonny Howard. I called it 'Sonny Howard's Blues.' And some other very original creations of mine.

Now, I also made some recordings with -- featuring Coleman Hawkins on Vanguard label, and on this particular session I had Earl Warren on alto saxophone, one of the old Count Basie men who was such a great first saxophone player, and along with Benny Morton on the trombone, who had also been with Count Basie and a great trombonist. And I had Joe Newman on trumpet, and I had -- let's see, O. C. Johnson on drums, and -- oh, I had -- I can't name all these musicians, but these were some of my most memorable recordings, along with
Coleman Hawkins being on my recordings. I had formerly played with him on his.
Right.
And he had come over and played some with mine. And one of the songs was an original piece that I had written featuring him.
What was it? I was --

It was called 'Under the Sweetheart Tree.' Actually it was written by my first wife, whose name was June Evans, and she played the piano, very beautiful classical piano, and she was interested in arranging and composing music. She was very highly inspired by Duke Ellington and Lionel Hampton, the combination of the two. And she was a very good classical pianist.

And I recorded this song that she wrote, and it was called 'Under the Sweetheart Tree,' featuring Coleman Hawkins on these Vanguard recordings. And it was these recordings with him, and the ones that I'd done with Charlie Parker earlier, which featured Charlie Parker as a member of my group, that to me were some of the highlights of my arranging and recording with my own group. You see what I mean?
Yes, I do. Can you think of any of the titles when you used Charlie Parker? Can you recall those titles?
Yeah, I told you awhile ago, 'Street
Beat, and some other. 'Tune Us In' and some others. Oh, yes, that's right.

Mostly original. '20th Century Blues,' which I considered to be my contribution to the modern ranging and composing which was going on during that time, which was comparable to Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker's thing, even though it was different. But what happened, after I made these recordings I went to California and I studied the organ because the organ was becoming popular then and I had heard Fats Waller play it in Tulsa, Oklahoma earlier, way when I was young.

And so I got interested in the organ, and I studied the organ for about three years, and I went back to New York and formed a group and played in Count Basie's bar. And from there I went to Europe with Buck --
Who did you have in that group, can you remember?

I had a saxophone player by the name of Percy France, a genius player, very wonderful player. And I had a drummer by the name of Danny Farrar, spelled F-a-r-r-a-r. He later went with Jonah Jones for awhile, good drummer, played with good feeling. And that was very exciting experience. And from there I had the pleasure of going to Europe with Buck Clayton and his fine group.
That was a wonderful band Buck had,
It was and --
Who all was in that?

It was Buck Clayton on trumpet and it was Emmett Berry on trumpet, and it was Dickie Wells on trombone, and there was Earle Warren on alto, and there was Buddy Tate on tenor, and there was --let's see on the bass there was -- who was the bass player. I can't remember the player.
Who was the drummer?
The drummer was Oliver Jackson.
Oh, yes. It's like a small Basie band.
Oh, it was a great band, and then Buck Clayton had written his music, and these fine arrangements that he's known for doing. And it was just really a wonderful experience.
It was a thrill then, wasn't it?
It was one of the highlights of my career.
Was it? You had tremendous reception everywhere, didn't you?
Not only that, but Buck Clayton was such a wonderful person, and he made it so pleasant to play. It was like the dream of playing with someone.
Isn't that wonderful.
And the music was great, and the tour
was highly successful.
That was wonderful.
And I enjoyed it to the greatest extent of enjoyment.
And then of course when you came back through the sixties, I mean after that you played clubs all over, didn't you?
Yes, the music --
Toronto and --

I played wherever I could find an engagement. The music business started to changing at that point, they were coming into this new found of rock and roll popularity and so forth. And so I just more or less strummed around as a solo player, you might say, [and] different clubs wherever I could find a booking. And the fact of the matter is I went back to my original playing solo piano, which I really enjoy because during these periods I get a chance to express myself more.

Well, you have so much -- you know, you have a great deal to offer, I mean, with all of that experience back of you there is that much more really that you can accomplish, I guess, after that much behind you, comparatively speaking. Wouldn't you say that's true?
Well, I don't know how to appraise
