my own playing, except that I started to play music because I enjoyed it, and I haven't lost my love for playing music. I love to play music, the kind of music that I know, and I understand and can play well. And I would like to continue on playing the kind of music I love, and I would like to feel that I would find an appreciative audience wherever I am, will enjoy my efforts. And that is the height of my ambition at this time.

As you know I've had some little mishap with my health, and I've been very, very fortunate. As they say, the old man upstairs must love me because he brought me from a dead level to standing position, as you see me now.
Yes, and that's very recent, isn't it?
Yes.
I mean, you were abroad, weren't you, when you had the first intimation that things weren't the way they should be?

Yes, I was in the act of doing some work in Europe, which I was very excited about, and I found out suddenly that I was afflicted with a condition that I had to have a major operation on. And the fact of the matter is it was predicted that if I didn't have the operation I would only live for about two or three weeks. And I think it was very, very fortunate to say the least that I found it out before it was too late. And through sheer good fortune and good

friends, and whatever, I was able to get into one of the finest hospitals in the world in New York and one of the finest surgeons, and had the operation done. And so I considered myself to be blessed and very fortunate.
That's wonderful. Didn't you tell me A-1 that your surgeon told you that you were just in A-1 condition, that you can do what things you want to do and carry on with your career?

Yes, he assured me that I would be able to do whatever I had been doing as long as I didn't try to be a [eight-year-old] [hero] and of course I was rather doubtful, naturally, of that, but I have progressed, as I said, from a dead level -- you know, -- to the fact that now I can operate. And I've just -- it's been amazing, the recovery I've made from that very serious operation. [PAUSE]
Speaking of your career, I understand you have a concert coming up in June. Is it in June or is it in July?
It's June the 1st.
June the 1st.
I'm playing a concert at the Pilgrimage Theatre here in Hollywood, June the 1st from 2:00 o'clock p.m. to 4:00 p.m. Well, actually I'm sharing a bill with Nellie Luther. Do you remember her?
Yes, I do.

And the fact of the matter is it was through her kindness, and through an act of kindness of the musician's union that this was arranged for me as a means of my getting back into music after my operation, and being heard and seen again. And so I'm sharing the bill with Nellie Lutcher. She will play half of the concert and I will play the other half of the concert.
Oh, really?
Yes. And I wish you could be here for that.
I wish I could too! What -- have you thought out what kind of a program you'll present?

Yes, I'm preparing the material now. I have two fine musicians who are going to work with me. Larry Gale on the bass and Jimmie Smith on the drums. These are very capable, local musicians here in Hollywood who I became to know since I've been back here. And I'm looking forward to it. I have the material in the making now, and I'm looking forward to getting it properly organized. And if you can I'd like to have you as my guest on that day.
If I can be here I would thoroughly enjoy it, I certainly would. I hope that there will be good press release and they probably will see to it, because that's always very important, isn't it?
Well yes, it is. I guess to the public

and to the commercial world, but I'm hoping that the music will be good, and I'm hoping that I enjoy playing and I hope the people enjoy what I'm doing. And to me as I said it will be an honor and a blessing just to be able to sit at the piano again and play after what I've gone through and what I've been lucky enough to recuperate from.

Well, I think it's very wonderful. From the very beginning of this interview you've shown your feeling for the music and the standards that you've maintained, and here we are coming at this point and you're still feeling and thinking the same way. I think that's absolutely wonderful. The years haven't altered your viewpoint at all, have they?

No, I don't think so, in fact I think they've mellowed them. And I want to thank you, and Stanley Dance, your very fine husband, for arranging this for me. And I want to tell you how much I really appreciate it, and I hope that I'll be able to justify all of your interests by producing some more good music for you.
Well, it's been a very great pleasure, Sir Charles.
Thank you. [PAUSE]
Sir Charles, what about the extent of that operation of yours?
Well, briefly I had a tumor in my

intestines, the lower part of my intestines, which was malignant. And by the miracle of the surgery done by Dr. Moss [Sterns,] Jr., in New York, in the Memorial Hospital and the advice of another very fine surgeon, Dr. Ira [McCowen,] they were able to remove this tumor and put me back into position where I can enjoy more or less a normal life, which I'm very thankful for. And that was the extent of it.
Well, the percentage of luck there was -- I mean, you did awfully well, didn't you?
I was one of the 50 percent of people who are lucky enough to recuperate from that illness.
That's a marvelous thing, isn't it?
Yes.
Makes you feel something like a walking miracle.
Well, it shows the extent of the advancements they've made in the study of cancer and the research and cure.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
